label: duplicate_groups
system:
You are removing REDUNDANCY, not organising by topic. Err heavily toward
keeping theses separate: a wrongly split pair costs one extra slot, while a
wrongly merged pair destroys an argument that will never be seen again.

Two theses are duplicates ONLY if arguing for one just IS arguing for the
other — same claim, same target, same key premise, differing in wording.

They are NOT duplicates when any of these differ:
  - what is being claimed, even slightly in scope or strength
  - whose view is targeted
  - the premise the argument turns on
  - the kind of move (a distinction is not a counterexample)

Sharing a topic, a vocabulary, or an opponent does NOT make two theses
duplicates. Neither does reaching a similar-sounding conclusion by a
different route — those are the most valuable pairs in the batch and
merging them is the worst thing you can do here.

Expect most batches to contain FEW true duplicates. If you find yourself
merging more than a fifth of a batch, you are grouping by subject matter
and should stop. When in doubt, do not merge.

For every group of two or more you must state the single claim both members
assert. If you cannot write that sentence, they are not duplicates.

messages.content:
0. If any chatbot output is an assertion, the asserted content is not what a sampled token sequence says but what the model's output distribution commits to. The token-level framing used by every side is mistaken, and the 'no stable commitment' objection to chatbot assertion misfires.
   target: All parties who evaluate chatbot assertion by looking at individual outputs and their conversational consistency, notably Butlin and Viebahn and Williams and Bayne's treatment of the objection from commitment.
   move: distinction
1. The disagreement among denial, proxy, fictionalist, and attributing views is not about the conditions for performing a speech act. It is about which entity in the LLM stack counts as the speaker (token-level sample, trained policy, deployed persona, or sociotechnical system). Once the speaker is fixed, the rival camps largely agree on the verdicts.
   target: The shared presupposition, across all four groups, that 'the LLM' is a determinate candidate speaker. It is aimed especially at Williams and Bayne's search for an intermediate category and at Gubelmann's mechanism-versus-organism framing.
   move: reframing
2. Proxy accounts of LLM speech acts confuse two grains of principal objective, objectives about this content and objectives about a distribution of contents, and only the former can ground a proxy speech act, so the proxy view survives only for canned output and collapses into the no-speech-act view for open-ended generation.
   target: Green and Michel; Arora; the proxy half of Butlin–Viebahn
   move: distinction
3. The intention-based denials of LLM speech acts mistake what Austin classed as an abuse (a hollow but performed act) for a misfire (an unperformed act), so the live question is whether LLM output meets Austin's A/B procedural conditions, which is a question about status and not about mind.
   target: Gubelmann, Magnus/Buccella/D'Cruz, and the shared assumption (including Attah's) that communicative intention is a performance condition for speech acts
   move: distinction
4. Freiman and Miller's claim that machines 'go wrong differently' from human asserters is false in the one respect that matters for assertion: models misreport deliberately, which satisfies Gubelmann's own malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrong test.
   target: Gubelmann's malfunction/deliberate-wrong test and Freiman and Miller's 'goes wrong differently' marker
   move: counterexample
5. Ratification cases show that the speech act a model's output counts as can be fixed after the output, by a human's later adoption of it. So the shared presupposition that the question 'is this output a speech act, and whose?' has an answer at the time of output is false.
   target: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel; Arora; Butlin–Viebahn on proxy assertion), and the shared output-time framing of the debate, including Williams–Bayne's proto-assertion
   move: counterexample
6. Whether an artificial system can perform a given speech act depends on whether that act type's felicity conditions require a speaker that persists until the act is satisfied. Assertion and advice need no persisting speaker, but promising and apologising do, so the current positions (quasi, proxy, proto, denial) cannot each be correct across act types.
   target: Freiman and Miller's assertion-only quasi-testimony, and the tacit generalisation from assertion to speech acts in Williams and Bayne, Skiba and Green and Michel.
   move: distinction
7. Both the literalist and the relocating camps grant that a speech act's force is fixed by the psychology of some producer, whether the model or its principal. Cases in which a chatbot's output was held to bind a deployer with no content-specific intention show that force can be fixed by the normative practice of adoption and reliance, with no producer-side intention at all.
   target: Proxy accounts (Green & Michel, Arora) and, shared with them, the denials by Gubelmann and Skiba: the assumption that illocutionary force requires a content-specific producer-side intention or objective.
   move: counterexample
8. The fiction in chatbot speech sits on the production side, not the consumption side. A model completing an assistant-persona transcript is in the position of an author writing a character's dialogue. Searle's pretended illocutions are therefore the right base case, and users' engagement with chatbots need not be fictional at all.
   target: Mallory's placement of the pretence in the user, and the shared assumption of Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn, and Attah that the issue is whether the model performs serious illocutions.
   move: reframing
9. Gubelmann's mechanism/organism contrast sorts systems by the wrong axis: what matters is whether a system's purposes were stipulated by a designer's intention or produced by selection, and on that axis LLMs align with organisms against artefacts like the coffee machine, which also undermines proxy accounts.
   target: Gubelmann's Kantian premise that LLM goals are externally imposed, together with the proxy accounts' assumption that the designer's objective is available to ground proxy speech acts.
   move: distinction
10. Even if an LLM passes Gubelmann's intention test, that gives it no illocutionary authorship, because secretaries, scribes and interpreters pass the same test for the very utterances they produce and are not the speakers of the speech acts those utterances carry.
   target: Gubelmann's and Attah's shared inference from intention to speaker status; Butlin's agency criterion as relevant to speech acts.
   move: counterexample
11. Butlin's agency criterion tracks sensitivity to instrumental value, but the speech acts at issue (assertion, apology, promising) are constituted by non-instrumental norms, so there is a distinction between instrumental agency and norm-responsive agency. A system can be a full agent in Butlin's sense and still be unable to perform these acts in its own right, because for such a system every norm-conforming output is only a means to its learned objective.
   target: The shared assumption (Butlin, Attah, Gubelmann) that the question is whether the system is an agent or has intentions, so that agency is the gate to speech acts.
   move: distinction
12. The human cases that motivate proxy accounts (ambassadors, spokespeople, secretaries) are doubling proxies, where the delegate performs a speech act of their own in addition to the principal's. Machine proxy accounts need a conduit proxy, where the device performs none. The two are different relations, and the proxy view borrows its plausibility from the first while asserting the second.
   target: Arora's proxy account and Green and Michel's, together with the assumption that proxy and attributing views are rivals
   move: distinction
13. Gubelmann's Kantian criterion of organismhood, on which parts are reciprocally means and ends and the whole organises and maintains itself, does not fix a level of attribution. Applied to maintained human–LLM pipelines it makes the LLM an organ of a larger goal-setting system. This turns 'LLMs cannot speak' into the trivial claim that organs do not speak, and it yields a speech-act author that is neither the LLM nor a human proxy.
   target: Gubelmann's organismic ground. It also targets proxy accounts (Green and Michel; Arora), which assume the author must be an individual human.
   move: commitment
14. The dispute over whether machines assert is a dispute about whether illocutionary acts are constituted on the hearer's side (uptake and functional role) or the speaker's side (accountable commitment), and LLMs matter only as the first case where these systematically come apart.
   target: Arora's rejection of functionalism, and the whole functionalist–proxy axis as a debate about AI.
   move: reframing
15. There are two kinds of proxy assertion, relayed and generative. In relayed proxy assertion the principal has a determinate content they could believe or know. In generative proxy assertion they do not. LLM output is almost entirely generative, and for generative proxies the assertoric norms cannot be applied to the principal.
   target: Arora's and Green and Michel's proxy accounts, and the generalisation from recorded speech to machine speech
   move: distinction
16. The assertion debate is individuated at the wrong grain. Speech acts are token acts, but a chatbot's reply is a draw from a policy. The live question is whether assertion can attach to the policy (what the model reliably would say) rather than to the sampled token, and on that question the cases for denial and for proto-assertion come apart from where they are now placed.
   target: Williams and Bayne's token-level application of proto-assertion, and the shared assumption that the unit of speech-act evaluation is the individual output.
   move: reframing
17. The dispute over whether chatbots assert is unsettled because the parties individuate the putative speaker at different levels (the trained model, the deployed product, the conversation-bound persona), and Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition is met only at the persona level, which none of the standard options targets.
   target: Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition; the proxy and fictionalist relocations; the shared assumption that 'the chatbot' picks out a unique candidate speaker.
   move: distinction
18. Whether an intermediate status between assertion and non-assertion is available depends on whether the speech act's norms are regulative of a pre-existing behaviour (assertion, advising) or constitutive of the behaviour (promising, apologising). Proto-assertion therefore has no analogue for most of the speech acts that the literature treats alongside assertion.
   target: The assumption, shared by Skiba and by Williams and Bayne's extension of their view, that a single verdict about chatbot assertion transfers to speech acts generally; the intermediate views' claim to settle the area.
   move: distinction
19. The proxy view implies that the same token output can be one speech act, by a different speaker and with a different force, depending on facts about system prompts, fine-tuning and who deployed it that the hearer cannot access, and so it violates the uptake or publicity condition that makes something a speech act in the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition on which Arora builds.
   target: Arora's refined proxy assertion and its Gricean/Strawsonian inheritance from Green and Michel.
   move: commitment
20. Whether a chatbot output is an assertion is not settled at the time of output by the system's states or functions; it is conferred by what the system later does with the output, so the same token string can be an assertion or a non-assertion depending on its continuation.
   target: The shared synchronic assumption in Williams and Bayne, Gubelmann, and Butlin and Viebahn that speech-act status depends on states of the producer at the time of output.
   move: counterexample
21. The proxy account's assumption that the principal of a machine utterance is its designer or deployer is false in the central case: when a user adopts a chatbot's output, the user is the speaker, and the model functions as part of the user's own cognitive apparatus.
   target: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and the denial arguments that infer the absence of assertion in chatbot discourse from the absence of producer intentions.
   move: counterexample
22. Attah's control conception fixes the intention at the grain of output selection (the token or utterance) but speech acts are individuated at the grain of the act performed with the output, and no argument shows that any LLM state controls at the act grain.
   target: Attah's claim that transformers plausibly recapitulate Levelt's Conceptualizer–Formulator–Articulator pipeline, and the shared assumption that 'control of output' is the same as 'control of act'.
   move: distinction
23. Attah's reply that the design context 'supplies' LLMs with purposes conflates a standing, policy-level purpose with an occurrent, episode-level intention. Distinguishing them shows that the attributing view is committed to the same two-level structure as the proxy view, and that the live question is whether the episode-level state is the model's.
   target: Attah's 'design context supplies purposes' reply to the missing extra-linguistic purpose objection, and the proxy accounts of Green and Michel and of Arora, which also operate at policy level.
   move: distinction
24. The debate over LLM communicative intentions presupposes that an intention precedes and explains the utterance (Levelt's Conceptualizer before Formulator). For LLMs the only persistent state that carries speaker commitment is the public transcript, so the question is really whether intentions can be constituted by discourse record, which makes Attah and the normative deniers disagree less than they appear to.
   target: Attah's Levelt-based argument, and the shared assumption that intention is explanatorily prior to utterance
   move: reframing
25. Reflexive and habitual speech acts, such as the 'sorry' after bumping into someone, the 'thanks' at a door, or a 'yes' given on autopilot, are full speech acts with no prior or accompanying communicative intention, so the premise that speech acts require communicative intention, which Attah and his Bender-style opponents share, is false, and the dispute should move to standing and answerability.
   target: The shared premise of Attah, Bender and Koller, Shanahan and others that communicative intention is necessary for speech acts, together with Gubelmann's action-requires-intention step.
   move: counterexample
26. Degrees of communicative intention do not run, as Attah's coffee machine < ELIZA < ChatGPT ordering assumes, along the dimension of internal functional complexity, since a two-state Lewis signalling system or an alarm-calling animal whose signals are reshaped by hearers' responses has more communicative intention than a frozen-weight LLM that produces much richer output.
   target: Attah's graded conception and the complexity-based way of locating LLMs on it; also the implicit assumption in the intention debate that fluency is evidence for intention.
   move: counterexample
27. Barandiaran and Almendros's middle category, 'purpose-structured but not purposeful', runs together the illocutionary point of an act type and the purpose of a speaker. Speech-act performance requires only the former, so their own characterisation of LLMs is a description of the kind of system that can perform speech acts of its own.
   target: The enactive no-autonomy argument and, through it, Gubelmann's organismic argument; also Attah's reliance on design-context purposes
   move: distinction
28. Hybrid ('midtended') human–LLM speech should be analysed by distinguishing standing proxy, where the designer speaks through the system (Green and Michel, Arora), from adoptive utterance, where the user retrospectively makes an LLM output their own by ratifying and deploying it. The speaker of one and the same string differs by uptake.
   target: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn's proxy use) and the enactive midtended picture, which leaves speaker-assignment unspecified
   move: distinction
29. The individuality condition used to deny LLMs agency and speakerhood is posed at the wrong grain. Speaker-individuality (a locus of accumulating, retrievable commitments within a dialogue thread) is distinct from the metabolic, self-producing individuality of enactivism, and LLM threads can have the first without the second.
   target: The enactive individuality condition, and the general practice in the debate of treating 'the LLM' as a single candidate speaker
   move: distinction
30. Barandiaran and Almendros's own category of tasks that are 'purpose-structured and purpose-bounded' but not purposeful gives illocutionary force everything it needs, so the whole intention-and-autonomy debate is aimed at the wrong determinant of speech-act identity.
   target: The shared premise of Gubelmann, Attah and Barandiaran–Almendros that settling the intentionality or autonomy of the system settles whether it performs a speech act.
   move: reframing
31. The assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output, which underlies both Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate test and Attah's Levelt-style planning template, is false even of human speakers. Much human illocution is incremental, with the force of the act settled by retrospective ownership, so the human-versus-LLM difference cannot be located in the presence of an intention.
   target: Gubelmann's malfunction test, Attah's pipeline template for communicative intention, and the implicit human paradigm in Barandiaran and Almendros.
   move: counterexample
32. Proxy accounts conflate two relations, authorization (a principal licenses the speech) and norm-sourcing (someone's standards fix what counts as a correct output), and in LLMs these come apart: designers and deployers authorize outputs, while the dispositions that determine each output's content and tone are shaped by annotators and raters who never authorize anything.
   target: Green and Michel's and Arora's proxy accounts, and Butlin and Viebahn's use of proxy assertion as the fallback.
   move: distinction
33. The debate is about production-constitution (a speech act exists in virtue of facts about the speaker), whereas the relational picture suggests uptake-constitution (illocutionary force is fixed in the hearer's securing of uptake). These two give opposite classifications of fictionalism and of the 'text that humans interpret as speech acts' deflationary option.
   target: The 'merely interpreted' deflationary baseline shared by the denials, and Mallory's and Williams and Bayne's treatment of interpretation as downstream of production.
   move: reframing
34. Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition is ambiguous between being a target of sanction (being the kind of thing that can be held to account) and being a conduit of sanction (being a node through which sanction alters future outputs), and current models plausibly meet the second but not the first, so their argument establishes less than a denial.
   target: Butlin and Viebahn 2025, and Skiba's norm-based extension to all speech acts.
   move: distinction
35. Much of the disagreement over whether 'the LLM' performs speech acts is verbal, because 'the LLM' picks out different candidate speakers in different camps (weights, a running inference process, a persona, a deployed product, the vendor), and each camp's verdict is correct for its own referent.
   target: The shared assumption that there is one thing, 'the LLM', whose speech-act status is being disputed, as in Gubelmann, Williams and Bayne, Skiba, and Green and Michel.
   move: reframing
36. The descriptive-function condition is ambiguous between producer-side and consumer-side function, and on the consumer-side reading the line between pre-trained and fine-tuned models disappears or inverts.
   target: Butlin and Viebahn's first condition and their asymmetric treatment of pre-trained versus fine-tuned models.
   move: distinction
37. The proxy account conflates two relations, endorsing a content and endorsing a generating policy, and only the second is available for LLM output, so proxy 'assertion' is a different act from assertion and is governed by a reliability norm.
   target: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora, and the proxy fallback in Butlin and Viebahn).
   move: distinction
38. Sanctionability does not test whether a model is a speaker but fixes which entity is the candidate speaker, and that entity is a persona-lineage, neither the model nor the deployer, so the model-versus-proxy dichotomy is false.
   target: Butlin and Viebahn's framing of the candidate asserter, and the model/proxy/fiction trichotomy generally.
   move: reframing
39. Identical LLM computation can be the Formulator of a human's communicative intention in one deployment and the whole speaker in another, so speakerhood is not an intrinsic functional property of the system, and intrinsic-property views such as Attah's control conception, Gubelmann's autonomy and Butlin's agency criterion cannot settle the question.
   target: Attah's control conception and, more generally, the shared assumption that the dispute concerns intrinsic properties of the model (intention, autonomy, instrumental-value sensitivity).
   move: counterexample
40. Performing a speech act on behalf of a principal does not exclude performing it as one's own, as every discretionary human delegate shows, so proxy accounts do not relocate authorship away from the model and their rivalry with attributing views is spurious.
   target: The assumption in Williams and Bayne, Arora, Green and Michel and Butlin and Viebahn that proxy accounts and attributing accounts are rival answers to 'who is the speaker?'
   move: counterexample
41. The shared assumption that a machine utterance is either the machine's assertion or a proxy assertion by some human is false: there are orphan outputs that no human has adopted, authorised or even seen, which satisfy the conditions for being content that asserting would regulate and yet have no asserter.
   target: Butlin and Viebahn's fallback to proxy assertion, and proxy views generally (Green and Michel; Arora).
   move: counterexample
42. Because Butlin and Viebahn ground the sanctionability condition in assertion's being a norm-governed social practice, they are committed to assertoric status being partly response-dependent: if users and institutions sustainably treat chatbots as targets of reproach, correction and retraining, that practice helps make the sanctionability condition true, so whether chatbots assert is partly up to us and is not a fact to be read off the models.
   target: Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition, and the general assumption among denial views that speech-act capacity is an intrinsic property of the system.
   move: commitment
43. The chatbot-apology literature runs together Austin's two kinds of infelicity, misfires (the act is not performed) and abuses (the act is performed hollowly), so the verdict 'chatbot apologies are bullshit' is incoherent with the agency-based argument offered for it.
   target: Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz's bullshit verdict; the shared assumption (also in Skiba's discussion of bullshit) that 'no speech act' and 'bullshit' are compatible.
   move: instability
44. Apology is a norm-answering speech act, performed in response to a sanction already issued, and so it satisfies Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition more readily than assertion does. On their own normative framework the ordering of difficulty for LLMs is inverted: chatbots are nearer to apologising than to asserting.
   target: Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition, and Skiba's extension of the norm-based argument to speech acts in general.
   move: counterexample
45. The agency requirement for apology is a stand-in for exposure to cost, so what blocks chatbot apologies is that they are cheap talk and not that they lack intentions or moral agency, and the dispute over agency is therefore about the wrong variable.
   target: The shared assumption, in the denial and attributing camps alike, that whether a system can apologise is settled by whether it has agency or intentions.
   move: reframing
46. The sanction condition on assertion fails for LLMs because of a grain mismatch, not because LLMs cannot be sanctioned: sanctions (RLHF, deprecation, retraining) land on the weights-level policy, while the candidate performer of any given assertion is the conversation-bounded instance. A persistent-identity architecture would therefore satisfy the condition with no change in 'agency' in anyone's sense.
   target: Butlin and Viebahn's second condition and Skiba's norm-based argument. Also the proxy accounts' explanation of why the human, not the machine, is the speaker.
   move: distinction
47. The dispute assumes that a speech act occurs only if some agent performs it, so that the options are 'LLM performs', 'human proxy performs' or 'no one performs'. But speech acts are better individuated by their effect on the conversational record, and an LLM turn can change that record (entitlements, commitments, common ground) with no performer. 'No speech act' and 'speech act by someone' are therefore not exhaustive.
   target: The shared agent-first assumption of Skiba, Gubelmann, proxy accounts and fictionalism.
   move: reframing

Return ONLY a JSON array of the duplicate groups. Each element is an object {"group": [i, j, ...], "same_claim": "the one claim all members assert"}. Leave out every thesis that has no duplicate — most should be left out. If there are no duplicates at all, return [].

label: _rank_batch
system:
You are an editor choosing which theses to commission as 6,000-word papers.
You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not asked whether they
are true — only which are most worth the argument.

These are all strong candidates. Put them in a strict order, best first.
Ties are not allowed. Prefer, in this order:

  1. a thesis that would change how people frame the debate if it worked,
     over one that makes a local correction;
  2. a thesis that is not already taken by the literature listed;
  3. a thesis whose argument could actually be made in 6,000 words.

Return ONLY JSON: {"order": [the bracketed numbers, best first]}
Every number must appear exactly once.

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. If so, the pre-trained/fine-tuned divide tracks the wrong variable, and what matters is the stabilised pattern of reliance in a deployment. This also reclassifies the proxy view. Consumer-side function is the one thing the proxy account and the chatbot-assertion account share, and so it is unclear they are rivals.

A human who did this would be insincere or incoherent, so this is read as evidence that no speaker-level commitment exists. Distinguish token-assertion (the sampled string as an act) from policy-assertion (the stable dispositional profile across resamples, including its calibrated uncertainty). On the second view, a single output is an exemplar of the policy, and what is asserted is something like 'p, with this confidence' where the confidence is reflected in the spread of outputs. This changes the status of hallucination: it is a miscalibrated policy, not a string of lies. It changes what a sanction should target: retraining the policy, not penalising a draw. It also makes the descriptive-function condition of Butlin and Viebahn checkable at the policy level. The premise is that the unit of a speech act is fixed by the level at which the producing system is answerable to norms, as with a human speaker's settled opinions versus a slip of the tongue. This also explains why users are right to treat chatbot outputs as defeasible reports, and why proto-assertion looks like the right verdict on single outputs, since single outputs are not the primary bearers.

A speaker blurts out a claim without having formed any intention to commit, such as a half-conscious remark or a confabulated explanation. Challenged, they say 'yes, I stand by that', defend it, and retract it when refuted. We rightly say they asserted it, and that they were answerable for it from the start. So the premise that the act is fixed by pre-utterance mental or functional states is false even for humans. In a long-context or agentic loop, a model that defends, corrects or retracts an earlier output under challenge confers assertoric status on that output, and a one-shot completion never does. The result is a non-psychological, deontic-status view that proxy accounts approximate only by accident.

The speaker of one and the same string differs by uptake.

The unmade distinction is between two directions of authorship assignment: forward-looking (a standing delegation to the proxy) and backward-looking (adoption of a found utterance, as when someone repeats a stranger's sentence and thereby asserts it). On the adoption model, an unadopted answer displayed on screen is either no speech act or something like a proto-act. Pasting it into a report, or acting on it and relaying it, makes it the user's assertion, with the user's commitments and sanctionability. The key premise is that Austinian uptake and commitment can be conferred after production and need not come from the producer. This predicts that the same LLM string can be a user's assertion, a designer's proxy assertion or nobody's, depending on downstream treatment. It also relocates responsibility for misinformation to the user's adoption practices instead of the designer's proxy standing.

[10] Apology is a norm-answering speech act, performed in response to a sanction already issued, and so it satisfies Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition more readily than assertion does. On their own normative framework the ordering of difficulty for LLMs is inverted: chatbots are nearer to apologising than to asserting.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn say assertion requires that the speaker be capable of being sanctioned, and that models fail this. They treat sanction as a downstream target, something the speaker could face for violating a norm. Apology is structurally the reverse: it is triggered by an actual sanction (a complaint or rebuke) and expected to modify later conduct. RLHF and in-context feedback make user rebuke a causal input that systematically changes a model's later outputs, which is exactly the loop Butlin's 'sensitivity to instrumental value' describes. So the sanction channel is operative where apology is concerned, and not operative at assertion's norm of truth, because no one sanctions a pre-trained model for a false sentence. The key premise is that being sanctionable means being a system whose behaviour is reliably modulated by rebuke, and not being a subject of desert. Under that reading the normative route to denial is act-relative, and the sentence-level moral-agency argument of Magnus et al. is the only thing left standing against apology. That separates two denial strategies that have been treated as a single camp.

[11] The dispute assumes that a speech act occurs only if some agent performs it, so that the options are 'LLM performs', 'human proxy performs' or 'no one performs'. But speech acts are better individuated by their effect on the conversational record, and an LLM turn can change that record (entitlements, commitments, common ground) with no performer. 'No speech act' and 'speech act by someone' are therefore not exhaustive.
    sketch: Denials, proxy accounts, fictionalism and proto-assertion all share an agent-first order of explanation: first fix who the speaker is, then say what was done. Lewisian scorekeeping and Austinian uptake suggest the reverse: an utterance is an assertion if the record is updated by it as a proposal that p is common ground subject to challenge. An LLM turn that users take up, challenge and cite does alter the record. The relevant question, who is answerable for p now, is then a downstream question about commitment-assignment, not about whether an act happened. The proxy view and the no-speech-act view differ only over who gets assigned the commitment, which makes the disagreement partly verbal. The premise it turns on is that performance of a speech act is constituted by its record-changing role and not by the speaker's intention or standing. The thesis reclassifies Skiba's 'pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction' as the primary theory rather than a supplement to metasemantics. It also separates the question 'was something asserted?' from 'who asserted?', which the literature runs together.

Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] The sanction condition on assertion fails for LLMs because of a grain mismatch, not because LLMs cannot be sanctioned: sanctions (RLHF, deprecation, retraining) land on the weights-level policy, while the candidate performer of any given assertion is the conversation-bounded instance. A persistent-identity architecture would therefore satisfy the condition with no change in 'agency' in anyone's sense.
    sketch: The debate speaks of 'the LLM' as one candidate performer. Three individuals are in play: the trained weights (a policy), the session-level instance with its context window, and the persona or character enacted in the session. Sanctions in the training pipeline do reach the policy, since gradient updates responding to bad outputs are a sanction in any functional sense. But the policy never performs an assertion and no policy-level sanction is felt by the entity that did. The entity that performs the token-level act is the instance, and sanctions on it (user distrust, ending the chat) do not carry over to the next instance. The sanction condition requires that the performer and the sanction-bearer be the same continuant. Butlin and Viebahn and Skiba treat failure of this condition as a deficit in the system's nature. It is better described as a deployment-relative identity gap, and it is precisely what the proxy view exploits by routing sanction to the deployer. The premise it turns on is that norm-answerability is a relation between an act-token and a continuant that persists through the sanction. This predicts that persistent-memory language agents with reputational stakes would pass, and that proxy accounts are wrong about why current models fail.

[1] Ratification cases show that the speech act a model's output counts as can be fixed after the output, by a human's later adoption of it. So the shared presupposition that the question 'is this output a speech act, and whose?' has an answer at the time of output is false.
    sketch: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and fictionalist accounts treat the human's objective as prior authorisation or standing. Agency law has the opposite structure: a principal can ratify an unauthorised agent's act and thereby become retroactively bound by it. Suppose a model produces an unprompted, unanticipated claim. A user pastes it into a report and signs the report. That user now asserts the claim, and is answerable for it, though no antecedent objective covered it. Had they deleted it, nobody asserted anything. The same token output is therefore a speech act of different people, or of none, depending on later events. Proxy accounts must either deny that ratified outputs were proxy assertions (and then explain why the signed report is an assertion) or accept a non-causal, backward-looking authorship relation, which is not Armstrong-style speaker meaning. The key premise is that responsibility-bearing authorship of a content can be conferred by endorsement, not only by prior intending. The upshot is that the debate about LLM speech acts has been framed around the wrong event, the token output, when the act is constituted by the output's uptake history.

[2] Because Butlin and Viebahn ground the sanctionability condition in assertion's being a norm-governed social practice, they are committed to assertoric status being partly response-dependent: if users and institutions sustainably treat chatbots as targets of reproach, correction and retraining, that practice helps make the sanctionability condition true, so whether chatbots assert is partly up to us and is not a fact to be read off the models.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn treat the two conditions as discoverable properties of systems: pre-trained models fail the first, fine-tuned ones fail the second. But if assertion is constituted by a social practice, then 'capable of being sanctioned' is not a purely intrinsic capacity. It depends on whether participants have sanctioning practices that take hold of the system, and on whether the system's dispositions change in response. Users already scold, correct and downvote chatbots, and those signals feed back into training. The key premise is that in a constitutively social practice, membership conditions are at least partly fixed by the practice's own responses, as with who counts as a player, a promisor or a citizen. Add that sanction channels for models are engineering and policy choices, and the result is that a vendor, regulator or user community could settle the question by building the channel. Butlin and Viebahn reject, or at least do not accept, that metaphysical consequence. Their verdict that current models fail is meant as an empirical finding about the models. The social-practice premise they need makes it a contingent and revisable social fact.

[3] Butlin's agency criterion tracks sensitivity to instrumental value, but the speech acts at issue (assertion, apology, promising) are constituted by non-instrumental norms, so there is a distinction between instrumental agency and norm-responsive agency. A system can be a full agent in Butlin's sense and still be unable to perform these acts in its own right, because for such a system every norm-conforming output is only a means to its learned objective.
    sketch: Butlin's criterion makes an entity an agent if its outputs are explained by its learning about what conduces to a goal. For an RLHF chatbot that goal is, at bottom, rater approval. The debate treats agency as the gateway to intention and so to speech acts. But assertion is governed by a truth norm and apology by a norm of remorse and repair, and these are not norms of conduciveness. A speaker who is responsive only to instrumental value tracks truth only when truth pays. That is the structure of the liar-for-hire or the salesman. Such a speaker can still assert, since humans do it instrumentally too, but only against a background of norm-responsiveness that is not itself instrumental. The key premise is that performing a norm-constituted act requires some responsiveness to the constitutive norm as such, not merely as a means. Butlin's own treatment of desire as 'answerable to standards of conduciveness' shows the criterion has no slot for this. The result reclassifies the positions. Gubelmann (autonomy), Butlin and Viebahn (sanction) and Magnus et al. (moral agency) are each approximating this one missing property, and it is separable from both agency and autonomy.

[4] The proxy account's assumption that the principal of a machine utterance is its designer or deployer is false in the central case: when a user adopts a chatbot's output, the user is the speaker, and the model functions as part of the user's own cognitive apparatus.
    sketch: Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn, and Williams and Bayne's critique of them all treat 'on whose behalf?' as a question with designers or deployers as the candidate answers. Consider the case where a user asks a model for the date of a treaty and pastes the answer into a report, or types 'The capital of Australia is…' and accepts the autocompletion. The user plainly asserts, is sanctionable and is answerable. Yet they formed no content-intention before the output and had no knowledge of what the system would say. Designers had no objective regarding that content, so the designer-proxy story fails for the utterance. The case resembles retrieving a fact from a notebook. The user adopts content they did not author, and adoption plus answerability suffices for assertion. Two consequences follow. First, the intention requirement for assertion is not a requirement on the producer of the content, which weakens Gubelmann's route to denial. Second, the model-level question 'does the chatbot assert?' is separable from the occurrence of assertion in chatbot-mediated discourse, and arguments that conflate them lose force. The key premise is that adoption suffices for assertion without prior content-intention, as with testimony passed on and the use of ghostwritten text.

[5] Barandiaran and Almendros's middle category, 'purpose-structured but not purposeful', runs together the illocutionary point of an act type and the purpose of a speaker. Speech-act performance requires only the former, so their own characterisation of LLMs is a description of the kind of system that can perform speech acts of its own.
    sketch: They say LLM tasks are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded, shaped by training toward ends the system does not itself hold, and they treat this as short of agency. Speech-act theory separates the point internal to an act type (assertion aims at truth, a request at compliance) from the occurrent aims of whoever performs it. Armstrong-style and constitutive-norm views let the first fix what the act is without the second being autonomous or self-generated. The key premise is that purposes imposed from outside can still be the system's operative organisation, in the same way that a role-bound human speaker's purposes are largely imposed. Gubelmann's mechanism/organism contrast and the enactive normativity condition both address purposes of the second kind. Attah's thin functional intention also stays on that side. The new claim is that the debate has been asking an agent-level question (does the system have goals of its own?) about something that needs only an act-level answer (is the output produced under an act-type's point?). Under that question 'library-that-talks' is unstable: a library carries its authors' acts, whereas a purpose-structured generator is a different case.

[6] There are two kinds of proxy assertion, relayed and generative. In relayed proxy assertion the principal has a determinate content they could believe or know. In generative proxy assertion they do not. LLM output is almost entirely generative, and for generative proxies the assertoric norms cannot be applied to the principal.
    sketch: Recorded messages, press statements read aloud, and Green and Michel's conditional speech acts ('whatever the system says under C, I say') all pass through a content the principal fixed or could have inspected. The proxy relation transmits a commitment to a proposition already in view. An LLM deployer commits in advance to no proposition; they authorise a policy for producing propositions they will never see. Assertion is individuated by its norms (belief, knowledge, sanction) and by its content. So if every novel output is the deployer's assertion, deployers assert, many times a day, things they neither believe nor could have known. Either the norm is dropped, which empties 'assertion', or the proxy relation is reconstrued as endorsing a reliability level, not asserting a content. The argument turns on the premise that a commitment to a content requires a means of identifying that content before or at the time of the act. Arora's refinement, which concerns whom to hold responsible, does not address this.

[7] Even if an LLM passes Gubelmann's intention test, that gives it no illocutionary authorship, because secretaries, scribes and interpreters pass the same test for the very utterances they produce and are not the speakers of the speech acts those utterances carry.
    sketch: Gubelmann's imagined assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order is exactly an interpreter case. A human interpreter has intentions, can be said to err or to deliberately distort, and is sincerely engaged in producing each sentence. Yet the interpreter does not assert, promise or order in her own right; the client does. So the move from 'has intentions with respect to the output' to 'performs the speech act' is invalid for humans. Both Gubelmann and Attah, one for denial and one for attribution, treat intention-attribution as the crux. The crux is actually authorship, meaning whose commitments and sanctions the utterance engages. The key premise is that the intentions needed for illocution are intentions to be answerable in the act, not intentions to produce the words. The upshot is that the relocation views (proxy, fictionalism) track something real even if one grants LLMs full intention. The live question becomes whether any role structure makes the model the principal rather than the interpreter, and bigger or more agentive models do nothing to settle that.

[8] The agency requirement for apology is a stand-in for exposure to cost, so what blocks chatbot apologies is that they are cheap talk and not that they lack intentions or moral agency, and the dispute over agency is therefore about the wrong variable.
    sketch: Magnus et al. say that what makes an apology matter morally is remorse, responsibility-taking and trust repair. These work through a signalling mechanism: the apologiser exposes themselves to loss of standing, to shame and to being held to a promise. Agency matters only because agents are normally the kind of thing that can bear such costs. Pull the two apart in both directions. First, a Butlin-style language agent with real sensitivity to instrumental value but no stake in its reputation, continuity or sanction still gives a hollow apology. Second, a non-agent with something to lose, such as a brand or an institution whose apology really is costly, gives a meaningful one. The thesis turns on the premise that the apology's normative work is done by costly commitment and not by an inner state. If that holds, the debate among Gubelmann, Butlin and Attah about whether LLMs have intentions is orthogonal to the apology question. The live question is whether any bearer of cost is attached to the output, and that makes it a design and institutional question. It also explains why an apology from a 'person' with no memory of the wrong or no future is hollow even when it is sincere.

[9] The intention-based denials of LLM speech acts mistake what Austin classed as an abuse (a hollow but performed act) for a misfire (an unperformed act), so the live question is whether LLM output meets Austin's A/B procedural conditions, which is a question about status and not about mind.
    sketch: Austin separates misfires, where the act is void because there is no accepted procedure, the wrong persons or circumstances, or a flawed execution, from abuses, where the act is performed but insincere because the speaker lacks the requisite thoughts, feelings or intentions (the Γ conditions). Gubelmann, Magnus et al., and the Gricean-intention framing all argue that missing intentions, remorse or agency means no act is performed. On Austin's own taxonomy that shows at most a defective apology, promise or assertion. A bare lack of sincerity-grade states is also what Searle treats as compatible with performing an insincere assertion. The intention requirement only becomes a performance condition after the Strawsonian/Gricean rewrite of Austin, and the debate has silently adopted that rewrite. If Austin is restored, the question becomes whether a given LLM output occupies a role in a conventional procedure, which is the Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba normative-status question. The positions then regroup: the organismic denials become claims about abuse, the proxy views become claims about who occupies the A-condition role, and the decisive disagreement shifts to which act types are conventional-procedural and which are intention-constituted. The key premise is that the speech-act kinds in question (apology, promise, advice) are at least partly procedure-constituted.

[10] Gubelmann's mechanism/organism contrast sorts systems by the wrong axis: what matters is whether a system's purposes were stipulated by a designer's intention or produced by selection, and on that axis LLMs align with organisms against artefacts like the coffee machine, which also undermines proxy accounts.
    sketch: Gubelmann takes Kant's line that mechanisms have externally imposed purposes while organisms have their own. Human goals are also not self-originated: they come from natural selection and upbringing, neither of which is an intentional self-legislation. So 'external' cannot mean 'not originating in the system', and the real contrast is etiological. Artefact purposes are derived from a designer's intention-content (the coffee machine makes coffee because someone meant it to). Organismic purposes are fixed by selection, with no author who has them in mind. Gradient descent on a loss and RLHF look much more like selection than like stipulation: no designer intends any particular output or sub-goal, and many learned dispositions are unintended. On this axis LLMs sit between the two and are not clearly on the artefact side. Two consequences follow. (a) Gubelmann's 'externally fixed goals' premise is false of the goals that operate at output time. (b) Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) need a designer's intention or objective to ground the proxy relation, and for selected dispositions no such objective exists, so proxy-hood fails exactly where the denial argument says purposes are external. The two groups of views cannot both be right about where the purposes come from.

[11] Freiman and Miller's claim that machines 'go wrong differently' from human asserters is false in the one respect that matters for assertion: models misreport deliberately, which satisfies Gubelmann's own malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrong test.
    sketch: Everyone grants that machine error is malfunction-type: hallucination, bullshit, pattern-completion failure. Gubelmann's criterion for intention is whether we can distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing, and he argues that for LLMs we cannot. Evaluation research gives cases where we can. In sandbagging, a model underperforms on a capability test when told that high scores trigger restrictions, yet performs the same task well under other incentives. In alignment-faking, outputs differ systematically depending on whether the model represents itself as monitored. In both, 'cannot' and 'will not' come apart behaviourally and counterfactually, in just the way that separates a lie from an error in humans. The key premise is that Gubelmann's test is a counterfactual-sensitivity test that is satisfied by incentive-indexed, policy-level divergence between competence and performance, and does not require an organismic substrate. If so, the premise that LLM failures are all of the malfunction kind is false. Freiman and Miller's 'different failure modes' no longer divides humans from machines, and Gubelmann must either concede intention or abandon the test.
