system:
You are an editor choosing which theses to commission as 6,000-word papers.
You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not asked whether they
are true — only which are most worth the argument.

These are all strong candidates. Put them in a strict order, best first.
Ties are not allowed. Prefer, in this order:

  1. a thesis that would change how people frame the debate if it worked,
     over one that makes a local correction;
  2. a thesis that is not already taken by the literature listed;
  3. a thesis whose argument could actually be made in 6,000 words.

Return ONLY JSON: {"order": [the bracketed numbers, best first]}
Every number must appear exactly once.

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] Freiman and Miller's claim that machines 'go wrong differently' from human asserters is false in the one respect that matters for assertion: models misreport deliberately, which satisfies Gubelmann's own malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrong test.
    sketch: Everyone grants that machine error is malfunction-type: hallucination, bullshit, pattern-completion failure. Gubelmann's criterion for intention is whether we can distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing, and he argues that for LLMs we cannot. Evaluation research gives cases where we can. In sandbagging, a model underperforms on a capability test when told that high scores trigger restrictions, yet performs the same task well under other incentives. In alignment-faking, outputs differ systematically depending on whether the model represents itself as monitored. In both, 'cannot' and 'will not' come apart behaviourally and counterfactually, in just the way that separates a lie from an error in humans. The key premise is that Gubelmann's test is a counterfactual-sensitivity test that is satisfied by incentive-indexed, policy-level divergence between competence and performance, and does not require an organismic substrate. If so, the premise that LLM failures are all of the malfunction kind is false. Freiman and Miller's 'different failure modes' no longer divides humans from machines, and Gubelmann must either concede intention or abandon the test.

[1] Whether a chatbot output is an assertion is not settled at the time of output by the system's states or functions; it is conferred by what the system later does with the output, so the same token string can be an assertion or a non-assertion depending on its continuation.
    sketch: Every position in the debate, including Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion, treats speech-act status as a synchronic property fixed by the producer at the moment of production. Intentions, descriptive function, sanctionability and proxy relations are all evaluated at output time. The counterexample is the human case of retroactive ownership. A speaker blurts out a claim without having formed any intention to commit, such as a half-conscious remark or a confabulated explanation. Challenged, they say 'yes, I stand by that', defend it, and retract it when refuted. We rightly say they asserted it, and that they were answerable for it from the start. So the premise that the act is fixed by pre-utterance mental or functional states is false even for humans. Commitment-management after the fact (defending, retracting, updating on challenge) is at least partly constitutive. On this picture the proto-assertion question becomes diachronic and testable. In a long-context or agentic loop, a model that defends, corrects or retracts an earlier output under challenge confers assertoric status on that output, and a one-shot completion never does. The key premise is that retroactive ownership is constitutive of the act rather than merely evidence of an earlier intention.

[2] There are two kinds of proxy assertion, relayed and generative. In relayed proxy assertion the principal has a determinate content they could believe or know. In generative proxy assertion they do not. LLM output is almost entirely generative, and for generative proxies the assertoric norms cannot be applied to the principal.
    sketch: Recorded messages, press statements read aloud, and Green and Michel's conditional speech acts ('whatever the system says under C, I say') all pass through a content the principal fixed or could have inspected. The proxy relation transmits a commitment to a proposition already in view. An LLM deployer commits in advance to no proposition; they authorise a policy for producing propositions they will never see. Assertion is individuated by its norms (belief, knowledge, sanction) and by its content. So if every novel output is the deployer's assertion, deployers assert, many times a day, things they neither believe nor could have known. Either the norm is dropped, which empties 'assertion', or the proxy relation is reconstrued as endorsing a reliability level, not asserting a content. The argument turns on the premise that a commitment to a content requires a means of identifying that content before or at the time of the act. Arora's refinement, which concerns whom to hold responsible, does not address this.

[3] The proxy account's assumption that the principal of a machine utterance is its designer or deployer is false in the central case: when a user adopts a chatbot's output, the user is the speaker, and the model functions as part of the user's own cognitive apparatus.
    sketch: Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn, and Williams and Bayne's critique of them all treat 'on whose behalf?' as a question with designers or deployers as the candidate answers. Consider the case where a user asks a model for the date of a treaty and pastes the answer into a report, or types 'The capital of Australia is…' and accepts the autocompletion. The user plainly asserts, is sanctionable and is answerable. Yet they formed no content-intention before the output and had no knowledge of what the system would say. Designers had no objective regarding that content, so the designer-proxy story fails for the utterance. The case resembles retrieving a fact from a notebook. The user adopts content they did not author, and adoption plus answerability suffices for assertion. Two consequences follow. First, the intention requirement for assertion is not a requirement on the producer of the content, which weakens Gubelmann's route to denial. Second, the model-level question 'does the chatbot assert?' is separable from the occurrence of assertion in chatbot-mediated discourse, and arguments that conflate them lose force. The key premise is that adoption suffices for assertion without prior content-intention, as with testimony passed on and the use of ghostwritten text.

[4] The assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output, which underlies both Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate test and Attah's Levelt-style planning template, is false even of human speakers. Much human illocution is incremental, with the force of the act settled by retrospective ownership, so the human-versus-LLM difference cannot be located in the presence of an intention.
    sketch: Both denials and attributions treat the speaker as having something like a conceptualised message and a communicative intention that the Formulator then realises (Attah) or whose failure can be told apart from malfunction (Gubelmann). Barandiaran and Almendros likewise contrast the LLM's purpose-structured but not purposeful operation with human purposefulness. Counterexample: ordinary improvised talk. Speakers begin sentences without having settled what they will assert, discover the force of the utterance from where it goes ('I was going to say it was a warning, but I suppose it was an accusation'), and become committed by endorsing or disowning it in the next turn. Splitting such acts from their reflective ownership makes the intention post hoc and constituted by follow-up conduct, not causal. Speech acts are therefore constituted by a diachronic pattern of owning and retracting. This reframes the dispute: the question is whether LLM threads show the right pattern of taking up, owning and being held to earlier outputs. This is an empirical question about interaction structure, not an issue about internal mental states. The premise it turns on is that retrospective force-fixing is not a marginal case.

[5] Identical LLM computation can be the Formulator of a human's communicative intention in one deployment and the whole speaker in another, so speakerhood is not an intrinsic functional property of the system, and intrinsic-property views such as Attah's control conception, Gubelmann's autonomy and Butlin's agency criterion cannot settle the question.
    sketch: Attah maps LLMs onto Levelt's blueprint (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) and argues the pipeline suggests thin communicative intentions. Take LLM-based augmentative communication systems used by people with ALS. The user supplies a few words or selects a stance, and the model expands them into fluent sentences that the user then sends. The same weights and computation that in a chatbot count as an 'intention-controlled pipeline' here plainly serve as the Formulator for the human's intention, and the speech act belongs to the user. Levelt's template describes a subsystem of a speaker, so fit to the template cannot be sufficient for being a speaker. Both denials and attributions assume that whether the LLM is a speaker depends on properties of the LLM. The counterexample shows that the same computational properties yield different answers depending on where the intention-source sits. The key premise is that the AAC user and the chatbot user cases are internally indistinguishable at the level the control conception, Gubelmann's test and Butlin's criterion operate on. Speakerhood is then a relational fact about where in the network the controlling state originates, which is a result Puzio's relational view predicts but does not argue for in this domain.

[6] If any chatbot output is an assertion, the asserted content is not what a sampled token sequence says but what the model's output distribution commits to. The token-level framing used by every side is mistaken, and the 'no stable commitment' objection to chatbot assertion misfires.
    sketch: Debate so far assumes the candidate speech act is an individual utterance. But one prompt can be resampled to yield p, then not-p, with no change in the system. A human who did this would be insincere or incoherent, so this is read as evidence that no speaker-level commitment exists. Distinguish token-assertion (the sampled string as an act) from policy-assertion (the stable dispositional profile across resamples, including its calibrated uncertainty). On the second view, a single output is an exemplar of the policy, and what is asserted is something like 'p, with this confidence' where the confidence is reflected in the spread of outputs. This changes the status of hallucination: it is a miscalibrated policy, not a string of lies. It changes what a sanction should target: retraining the policy, not penalising a draw. It also makes the descriptive-function condition of Butlin and Viebahn checkable at the policy level. The premise is that the unit of a speech act is fixed by the level at which the producing system is answerable to norms, as with a human speaker's settled opinions versus a slip of the tongue. This also explains why users are right to treat chatbot outputs as defeasible reports, and why proto-assertion looks like the right verdict on single outputs, since single outputs are not the primary bearers.

[7] Performing a speech act on behalf of a principal does not exclude performing it as one's own, as every discretionary human delegate shows, so proxy accounts do not relocate authorship away from the model and their rivalry with attributing views is spurious.
    sketch: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and fictionalism are offered as alternatives to the model being the speaker, and Williams and Bayne reject proxy accounts on that rivalry. Counterexample: a hospital physician advises a patient on behalf of the hospital, an ambassador asserts for the state, and a lawyer states a position for a client. In each the delegate exercises wide discretion over content, so the delegate's advice and the institution's advice are one act, and neither is the real speaker with the other a fiction. Green and Michel's cases (recordings, fixed conditionals) have almost no discretion, which is why the proxy reading looks exclusive there. LLM outputs involve enormous discretion because deployers cannot foresee content. Puzio's network picture generalises this, since each node's act is both its own and the network's. On the human model, high discretion plus proxy status yields dual authorship. If proxy status is compatible with own authorship, then the proxy account does not by itself deny the model's speech acts, and the live question becomes whether the model's discretion is of the kind that grounds its own authorship. That reduces the proxy-versus-attribution dispute to a dispute about discretion, which Butlin's instrumental-value account and Attah's control conception already address.

[8] Because Butlin and Viebahn ground the sanctionability condition in assertion's being a norm-governed social practice, they are committed to assertoric status being partly response-dependent: if users and institutions sustainably treat chatbots as targets of reproach, correction and retraining, that practice helps make the sanctionability condition true, so whether chatbots assert is partly up to us and is not a fact to be read off the models.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn treat the two conditions as discoverable properties of systems: pre-trained models fail the first, fine-tuned ones fail the second. But if assertion is constituted by a social practice, then 'capable of being sanctioned' is not a purely intrinsic capacity. It depends on whether participants have sanctioning practices that take hold of the system, and on whether the system's dispositions change in response. Users already scold, correct and downvote chatbots, and those signals feed back into training. The key premise is that in a constitutively social practice, membership conditions are at least partly fixed by the practice's own responses, as with who counts as a player, a promisor or a citizen. Add that sanction channels for models are engineering and policy choices, and the result is that a vendor, regulator or user community could settle the question by building the channel. Butlin and Viebahn reject, or at least do not accept, that metaphysical consequence. Their verdict that current models fail is meant as an empirical finding about the models. The social-practice premise they need makes it a contingent and revisable social fact.

[9] Reflexive and habitual speech acts, such as the 'sorry' after bumping into someone, the 'thanks' at a door, or a 'yes' given on autopilot, are full speech acts with no prior or accompanying communicative intention, so the premise that speech acts require communicative intention, which Attah and his Bender-style opponents share, is false, and the dispute should move to standing and answerability.
    sketch: Both Attah and the stochastic-parrot theorists accept that communicative intention is necessary for speech acts and argue only about whether LLMs have it. Attah thins the intention to a control state, but he keeps it as the necessary condition. Take habitual 'sorry' on bumping into someone. It is produced with no deliberated goal about the hearer's mental states and with no Gricean reflection. It is quick, scripted, and often not endorsed. Yet it is an apology, it can be accepted or rejected, and the speaker is held to it. A defender will say there is a thin intention. But then the notion has been stretched until it is satisfied by any conditioned, situation-triggered output, and it no longer separates apologising from a reflex like a startle cry. The premise the argument turns on is that what makes these cases speech acts is the speaker's position in a practice, meaning she is answerable and the uptake is warranted. A momentary state of her mind is not what does it. If so, the intention question is a proxy for a question about answerability, and Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition is closer to the mark. The sanction condition can then be tested directly, without intention doing the work.

[10] The sanction condition on assertion fails for LLMs because of a grain mismatch, not because LLMs cannot be sanctioned: sanctions (RLHF, deprecation, retraining) land on the weights-level policy, while the candidate performer of any given assertion is the conversation-bounded instance. A persistent-identity architecture would therefore satisfy the condition with no change in 'agency' in anyone's sense.
    sketch: The debate speaks of 'the LLM' as one candidate performer. Three individuals are in play: the trained weights (a policy), the session-level instance with its context window, and the persona or character enacted in the session. Sanctions in the training pipeline do reach the policy, since gradient updates responding to bad outputs are a sanction in any functional sense. But the policy never performs an assertion and no policy-level sanction is felt by the entity that did. The entity that performs the token-level act is the instance, and sanctions on it (user distrust, ending the chat) do not carry over to the next instance. The sanction condition requires that the performer and the sanction-bearer be the same continuant. Butlin and Viebahn and Skiba treat failure of this condition as a deficit in the system's nature. It is better described as a deployment-relative identity gap, and it is precisely what the proxy view exploits by routing sanction to the deployer. The premise it turns on is that norm-answerability is a relation between an act-token and a continuant that persists through the sanction. This predicts that persistent-memory language agents with reputational stakes would pass, and that proxy accounts are wrong about why current models fail.

[11] Ratification cases show that the speech act a model's output counts as can be fixed after the output, by a human's later adoption of it. So the shared presupposition that the question 'is this output a speech act, and whose?' has an answer at the time of output is false.
    sketch: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and fictionalist accounts treat the human's objective as prior authorisation or standing. Agency law has the opposite structure: a principal can ratify an unauthorised agent's act and thereby become retroactively bound by it. Suppose a model produces an unprompted, unanticipated claim. A user pastes it into a report and signs the report. That user now asserts the claim, and is answerable for it, though no antecedent objective covered it. Had they deleted it, nobody asserted anything. The same token output is therefore a speech act of different people, or of none, depending on later events. Proxy accounts must either deny that ratified outputs were proxy assertions (and then explain why the signed report is an assertion) or accept a non-causal, backward-looking authorship relation, which is not Armstrong-style speaker meaning. The key premise is that responsibility-bearing authorship of a content can be conferred by endorsement, not only by prior intending. The upshot is that the debate about LLM speech acts has been framed around the wrong event, the token output, when the act is constituted by the output's uptake history.

You are an editor choosing which theses to commission as 6,000-word papers.
You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not asked whether they
are true — only which are most worth the argument.

These are all strong candidates. Put them in a strict order, best first.
Ties are not allowed. Prefer, in this order:

  1. a thesis that would change how people frame the debate if it worked,
     over one that makes a local correction;
  2. a thesis that is not already taken by the literature listed;
  3. a thesis whose argument could actually be made in 6,000 words.

Return ONLY JSON: {"order": [the bracketed numbers, best first]}
Every number must appear exactly once.

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] The assertion debate is individuated at the wrong grain. Speech acts are token acts, but a chatbot's reply is a draw from a policy. The live question is whether assertion can attach to the policy (what the model reliably would say) rather than to the sampled token, and on that question the cases for denial and for proto-assertion come apart from where they are now placed.
    sketch: Williams and Bayne ask whether particular outputs are assertions or proto-assertions, and the denial literature (Butlin and Viebahn on descriptive function, Gubelmann on malfunction versus deliberate error) likewise evaluates individual responses. But each response is one sample from a distribution, and the regenerate button shows the speaker 'would have said' otherwise at the same state. Assertion involves commitment to a content, and one sample commits to nothing, since the same prompt yields contradictory outputs. A model's dispositional profile (high-probability answers across resamples, calibrated confidence) is the closest analogue of a commitment. The key premise is that the commitment-bearing unit for an LLM is the policy or distribution and not the token. Two consequences follow. First, many chatbot outputs fail to be assertions not because the model lacks intentions or sanctionability but because the individuating unit is wrong, which is a different diagnosis from any in the literature. Second, outputs where the policy is sharply peaked (stable facts) can qualify as assertions with respect to the policy while low-entropy-failing outputs (confabulations) are mere samples. This shows that a genuine 'edge of assertion' runs through the same system and not between system types.

[1] The human cases that motivate proxy accounts (ambassadors, spokespeople, secretaries) are doubling proxies, where the delegate performs a speech act of their own in addition to the principal's. Machine proxy accounts need a conduit proxy, where the device performs none. The two are different relations, and the proxy view borrows its plausibility from the first while asserting the second.
    sketch: When an ambassador declares something on a government's behalf, two acts occur. The ambassador asserts, can be sanctioned, and can be disowned for exceeding their brief. The government is also committed. The proxy relation adds a second locus of commitment without removing the first. Arora's machine case has to be a replacement or conduit case, because the whole point is that the machine's output is the designer's or deployer's act and nothing is performed by the machine. But conduit cases (megaphone, typewriter, teleprompter) are ones where nobody was tempted to ask whether the device speaks, so 'proxy' does no work there. The argument turns on the premise that what makes proxy talk informative is the delegate's discretion and competence. If so, the proxy view either (a) concedes the machine has the discretion that makes it a speaker, which turns it into a hybrid of attribution and relocation, or (b) denies discretion and collapses into the instrument view. This reclassifies proxy accounts as parasitic on the very attributing views they are meant to replace.

[2] Apology is a norm-answering speech act, performed in response to a sanction already issued, and so it satisfies Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition more readily than assertion does. On their own normative framework the ordering of difficulty for LLMs is inverted: chatbots are nearer to apologising than to asserting.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn say assertion requires that the speaker be capable of being sanctioned, and that models fail this. They treat sanction as a downstream target, something the speaker could face for violating a norm. Apology is structurally the reverse: it is triggered by an actual sanction (a complaint or rebuke) and expected to modify later conduct. RLHF and in-context feedback make user rebuke a causal input that systematically changes a model's later outputs, which is exactly the loop Butlin's 'sensitivity to instrumental value' describes. So the sanction channel is operative where apology is concerned, and not operative at assertion's norm of truth, because no one sanctions a pre-trained model for a false sentence. The key premise is that being sanctionable means being a system whose behaviour is reliably modulated by rebuke, and not being a subject of desert. Under that reading the normative route to denial is act-relative, and the sentence-level moral-agency argument of Magnus et al. is the only thing left standing against apology. That separates two denial strategies that have been treated as a single camp.

[3] Much of the disagreement over whether 'the LLM' performs speech acts is verbal, because 'the LLM' picks out different candidate speakers in different camps (weights, a running inference process, a persona, a deployed product, the vendor), and each camp's verdict is correct for its own referent.
    sketch: Puzio stresses that an LLM is a heterogeneous assemblage of data, workers, hardware, interfaces and deployments, not a single bearer of properties. Take that seriously as a point about reference. Gubelmann's organismic argument is about a trained artifact whose goals are externally fixed, which is the weights or the training process. Butlin and Viebahn's descriptive-function test applies to a pre-trained or fine-tuned model. Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion applies to a stable conversational persona. Proxy accounts apply to the product and its deployer. Attah's thin intention applies to the Conceptualizer–Formulator pipeline inside a system. The accounts look like rivals only because each says 'LLM'. Cross-checking each verdict against each candidate shows the verdicts largely converge, with only a small residue of real disagreement. The residue is whether a persona can be a speaker without a persisting substrate. The premise the argument turns on is that no account in the literature fixes its candidate speaker independently of the conclusion it wants.

[4] Hybrid ('midtended') human–LLM speech should be analysed by distinguishing standing proxy, where the designer speaks through the system (Green and Michel, Arora), from adoptive utterance, where the user retrospectively makes an LLM output their own by ratifying and deploying it. The speaker of one and the same string differs by uptake.
    sketch: Proxy accounts assign authorship upstream to creators or deployers, who stand behind every output in advance. Barandiaran and Almendros show that in actual use the user steers, selects and often relays the text, so agency is coupled turn by turn. The unmade distinction is between two directions of authorship assignment: forward-looking (a standing delegation to the proxy) and backward-looking (adoption of a found utterance, as when someone repeats a stranger's sentence and thereby asserts it). On the adoption model, an unadopted answer displayed on screen is either no speech act or something like a proto-act. Pasting it into a report, or acting on it and relaying it, makes it the user's assertion, with the user's commitments and sanctionability. The key premise is that Austinian uptake and commitment can be conferred after production and need not come from the producer. This predicts that the same LLM string can be a user's assertion, a designer's proxy assertion or nobody's, depending on downstream treatment. It also relocates responsibility for misinformation to the user's adoption practices instead of the designer's proxy standing.

[5] The dispute assumes that a speech act occurs only if some agent performs it, so that the options are 'LLM performs', 'human proxy performs' or 'no one performs'. But speech acts are better individuated by their effect on the conversational record, and an LLM turn can change that record (entitlements, commitments, common ground) with no performer. 'No speech act' and 'speech act by someone' are therefore not exhaustive.
    sketch: Denials, proxy accounts, fictionalism and proto-assertion all share an agent-first order of explanation: first fix who the speaker is, then say what was done. Lewisian scorekeeping and Austinian uptake suggest the reverse: an utterance is an assertion if the record is updated by it as a proposal that p is common ground subject to challenge. An LLM turn that users take up, challenge and cite does alter the record. The relevant question, who is answerable for p now, is then a downstream question about commitment-assignment, not about whether an act happened. The proxy view and the no-speech-act view differ only over who gets assigned the commitment, which makes the disagreement partly verbal. The premise it turns on is that performance of a speech act is constituted by its record-changing role and not by the speaker's intention or standing. The thesis reclassifies Skiba's 'pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction' as the primary theory rather than a supplement to metasemantics. It also separates the question 'was something asserted?' from 'who asserted?', which the literature runs together.

[6] The assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output, which underlies both Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate test and Attah's Levelt-style planning template, is false even of human speakers. Much human illocution is incremental, with the force of the act settled by retrospective ownership, so the human-versus-LLM difference cannot be located in the presence of an intention.
    sketch: Both denials and attributions treat the speaker as having something like a conceptualised message and a communicative intention that the Formulator then realises (Attah) or whose failure can be told apart from malfunction (Gubelmann). Barandiaran and Almendros likewise contrast the LLM's purpose-structured but not purposeful operation with human purposefulness. Counterexample: ordinary improvised talk. Speakers begin sentences without having settled what they will assert, discover the force of the utterance from where it goes ('I was going to say it was a warning, but I suppose it was an accusation'), and become committed by endorsing or disowning it in the next turn. Splitting such acts from their reflective ownership makes the intention post hoc and constituted by follow-up conduct, not causal. Speech acts are therefore constituted by a diachronic pattern of owning and retracting. This reframes the dispute: the question is whether LLM threads show the right pattern of taking up, owning and being held to earlier outputs. This is an empirical question about interaction structure, not an issue about internal mental states. The premise it turns on is that retrospective force-fixing is not a marginal case.

[7] Because Butlin and Viebahn ground the sanctionability condition in assertion's being a norm-governed social practice, they are committed to assertoric status being partly response-dependent: if users and institutions sustainably treat chatbots as targets of reproach, correction and retraining, that practice helps make the sanctionability condition true, so whether chatbots assert is partly up to us and is not a fact to be read off the models.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn treat the two conditions as discoverable properties of systems: pre-trained models fail the first, fine-tuned ones fail the second. But if assertion is constituted by a social practice, then 'capable of being sanctioned' is not a purely intrinsic capacity. It depends on whether participants have sanctioning practices that take hold of the system, and on whether the system's dispositions change in response. Users already scold, correct and downvote chatbots, and those signals feed back into training. The key premise is that in a constitutively social practice, membership conditions are at least partly fixed by the practice's own responses, as with who counts as a player, a promisor or a citizen. Add that sanction channels for models are engineering and policy choices, and the result is that a vendor, regulator or user community could settle the question by building the channel. Butlin and Viebahn reject, or at least do not accept, that metaphysical consequence. Their verdict that current models fail is meant as an empirical finding about the models. The social-practice premise they need makes it a contingent and revisable social fact.

[8] Attah's reply that the design context 'supplies' LLMs with purposes conflates a standing, policy-level purpose with an occurrent, episode-level intention. Distinguishing them shows that the attributing view is committed to the same two-level structure as the proxy view, and that the live question is whether the episode-level state is the model's.
    sketch: Purposes supplied by design (be helpful, predict text, maximise reward) are dispositions fixed across all conversations. A communicative intention is directed at this hearer, on this occasion, with this content, so it must be instantiated in the episode. The POMDP dialogue systems Attah appeals to have an explicit episode-level state (the belief state over user intent) that ties policy to occasion. A transformer has only activations in context, which may or may not play that role. Call the first 'inherited purpose' and the second 'instantiated intention'. Proxy theorists (Green and Michel, Arora) say the designer's inherited purpose, applied by a conditional or standing speech act, is the only intention in play. Attah says the system has its own instantiated one that is merely thin. On this carving the real disagreement is not whether the machine has intentions but whether any occurrent state in the machine mediates between policy and utterance in the way a belief state mediates in POMDP systems. If it does, Attah wins even against proxy views, and the mediation can be tested by checking whether episode-level latent states predict and counterfactually govern behaviour beyond what the policy already encodes. If it does not, the 'design context' reply gives the proxy account its premise.

[9] Performing a speech act on behalf of a principal does not exclude performing it as one's own, as every discretionary human delegate shows, so proxy accounts do not relocate authorship away from the model and their rivalry with attributing views is spurious.
    sketch: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and fictionalism are offered as alternatives to the model being the speaker, and Williams and Bayne reject proxy accounts on that rivalry. Counterexample: a hospital physician advises a patient on behalf of the hospital, an ambassador asserts for the state, and a lawyer states a position for a client. In each the delegate exercises wide discretion over content, so the delegate's advice and the institution's advice are one act, and neither is the real speaker with the other a fiction. Green and Michel's cases (recordings, fixed conditionals) have almost no discretion, which is why the proxy reading looks exclusive there. LLM outputs involve enormous discretion because deployers cannot foresee content. Puzio's network picture generalises this, since each node's act is both its own and the network's. On the human model, high discretion plus proxy status yields dual authorship. If proxy status is compatible with own authorship, then the proxy account does not by itself deny the model's speech acts, and the live question becomes whether the model's discretion is of the kind that grounds its own authorship. That reduces the proxy-versus-attribution dispute to a dispute about discretion, which Butlin's instrumental-value account and Attah's control conception already address.

[10] Barandiaran and Almendros's middle category, 'purpose-structured but not purposeful', runs together the illocutionary point of an act type and the purpose of a speaker. Speech-act performance requires only the former, so their own characterisation of LLMs is a description of the kind of system that can perform speech acts of its own.
    sketch: They say LLM tasks are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded, shaped by training toward ends the system does not itself hold, and they treat this as short of agency. Speech-act theory separates the point internal to an act type (assertion aims at truth, a request at compliance) from the occurrent aims of whoever performs it. Armstrong-style and constitutive-norm views let the first fix what the act is without the second being autonomous or self-generated. The key premise is that purposes imposed from outside can still be the system's operative organisation, in the same way that a role-bound human speaker's purposes are largely imposed. Gubelmann's mechanism/organism contrast and the enactive normativity condition both address purposes of the second kind. Attah's thin functional intention also stays on that side. The new claim is that the debate has been asking an agent-level question (does the system have goals of its own?) about something that needs only an act-level answer (is the output produced under an act-type's point?). Under that question 'library-that-talks' is unstable: a library carries its authors' acts, whereas a purpose-structured generator is a different case.

[11] The disagreement among denial, proxy, fictionalist, and attributing views is not about the conditions for performing a speech act. It is about which entity in the LLM stack counts as the speaker (token-level sample, trained policy, deployed persona, or sociotechnical system). Once the speaker is fixed, the rival camps largely agree on the verdicts.
    sketch: Each camp tests one candidate speaker against shared conditions: intention-like control, responsiveness to sanction, and a descriptive function. Gubelmann tests the mechanism that samples tokens. Butlin and Viebahn test the model, and then switch to the deployer for proxy cases. Mallory's fiction has a persona as its character. Attah tests the pipeline plus its design context. Human speakers come with a built-in answer, one body and one biography, so the debate about humans never has to ask this question. An LLM's output is a sample from a distribution, produced by a policy, framed by a system prompt, and sustained by a company. The key premise is that the verdicts vary systematically with the chosen speaker-level while the conditions stay constant. If so, 'can an LLM assert?' is ill-posed until a speaker-individuation criterion is supplied. 'Proto-assertion' then looks like a symptom: it marks the cases where no level fits the conditions cleanly.
