system:
You are an editor choosing which theses to commission as 6,000-word papers.
You have NOT seen any of them attacked, and you are not asked whether they
are true — only which are most worth the argument.

These are all strong candidates. Put them in a strict order, best first.
Ties are not allowed. Prefer, in this order:

  1. a thesis that would change how people frame the debate if it worked,
     over one that makes a local correction;
  2. a thesis that is not already taken by the literature listed;
  3. a thesis whose argument could actually be made in 6,000 words.

Return ONLY JSON: {"order": [the bracketed numbers, best first]}
Every number must appear exactly once.

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] The sanction condition on assertion fails for LLMs because of a grain mismatch, not because LLMs cannot be sanctioned: sanctions (RLHF, deprecation, retraining) land on the weights-level policy, while the candidate performer of any given assertion is the conversation-bounded instance. A persistent-identity architecture would therefore satisfy the condition with no change in 'agency' in anyone's sense.
    sketch: The debate speaks of 'the LLM' as one candidate performer. Three individuals are in play: the trained weights (a policy), the session-level instance with its context window, and the persona or character enacted in the session. Sanctions in the training pipeline do reach the policy, since gradient updates responding to bad outputs are a sanction in any functional sense. But the policy never performs an assertion and no policy-level sanction is felt by the entity that did. The entity that performs the token-level act is the instance, and sanctions on it (user distrust, ending the chat) do not carry over to the next instance. The sanction condition requires that the performer and the sanction-bearer be the same continuant. Butlin and Viebahn and Skiba treat failure of this condition as a deficit in the system's nature. It is better described as a deployment-relative identity gap, and it is precisely what the proxy view exploits by routing sanction to the deployer. The premise it turns on is that norm-answerability is a relation between an act-token and a continuant that persists through the sanction. This predicts that persistent-memory language agents with reputational stakes would pass, and that proxy accounts are wrong about why current models fail.

[1] The debate over LLM communicative intentions presupposes that an intention precedes and explains the utterance (Levelt's Conceptualizer before Formulator). For LLMs the only persistent state that carries speaker commitment is the public transcript, so the question is really whether intentions can be constituted by discourse record, which makes Attah and the normative deniers disagree less than they appear to.
    sketch: Attah maps transformers onto Levelt's pipeline and says the intention is a prior internal controller. But an autoregressive model has no separate pre-verbal message that persists across the generation. At each step the only thing carried forward is the text produced so far (plus the cache). What binds the system to its earlier output, such as a claim it must stay consistent with or an apology it has issued, is the transcript, which is shared and inspectable by the user. So whatever 'intention' the model has is largely retroactively and publicly fixed by what it has already said, much as Anscombe, Brandom and the interpretivists treat intention as answerable to the record of performance. The premise the argument turns on is that, for LLMs, intention-as-prior-inner-state and commitment-as-public-score come apart and only the second is robustly present. Then Attah's 'thin' attribution and Butlin and Viebahn's social-practice condition describe the same structure from two sides. The real contest is between inner-priority and record-constitution accounts of intention, and humans are only a contingent instance of the former.

[2] If any chatbot output is an assertion, the asserted content is not what a sampled token sequence says but what the model's output distribution commits to. The token-level framing used by every side is mistaken, and the 'no stable commitment' objection to chatbot assertion misfires.
    sketch: Debate so far assumes the candidate speech act is an individual utterance. But one prompt can be resampled to yield p, then not-p, with no change in the system. A human who did this would be insincere or incoherent, so this is read as evidence that no speaker-level commitment exists. Distinguish token-assertion (the sampled string as an act) from policy-assertion (the stable dispositional profile across resamples, including its calibrated uncertainty). On the second view, a single output is an exemplar of the policy, and what is asserted is something like 'p, with this confidence' where the confidence is reflected in the spread of outputs. This changes the status of hallucination: it is a miscalibrated policy, not a string of lies. It changes what a sanction should target: retraining the policy, not penalising a draw. It also makes the descriptive-function condition of Butlin and Viebahn checkable at the policy level. The premise is that the unit of a speech act is fixed by the level at which the producing system is answerable to norms, as with a human speaker's settled opinions versus a slip of the tongue. This also explains why users are right to treat chatbot outputs as defeasible reports, and why proto-assertion looks like the right verdict on single outputs, since single outputs are not the primary bearers.

[3] Both the literalist and the relocating camps grant that a speech act's force is fixed by the psychology of some producer, whether the model or its principal. Cases in which a chatbot's output was held to bind a deployer with no content-specific intention show that force can be fixed by the normative practice of adoption and reliance, with no producer-side intention at all.
    sketch: Take Moffatt v. Air Canada, where a tribunal held the airline to its chatbot's statement of a bereavement-fare policy. No designer or deployer had any objective regarding that content, so Green and Michel's Armstrong-style 'objectives' condition for proxy speech acts fails. The tribunal also did not treat the utterance as fiction or as mere signalling, so Mallory's fictionalism misdescribes the practice. The objective theory of contract and of representation gives the general pattern: an utterance counts as a promise or assertion by an agent because of the agent's role, the uptake, and the allocation of risk, whatever the agent intended. The key premise is that this is a case of illocution and not merely of liability. The evidence is that the standard felicity vocabulary applies: the statement is 'a misrepresentation', 'a promise', and so on. If that holds, the question 'who is the author of the model's speech act?' is badly posed. Authorship is conferred by the practice and not discovered in the producer's mind. The result is a non-psychological, deontic-status view that proxy accounts approximate only by accident.

[4] Whether an artificial system can perform a given speech act depends on whether that act type's felicity conditions require a speaker that persists until the act is satisfied. Assertion and advice need no persisting speaker, but promising and apologising do, so the current positions (quasi, proxy, proto, denial) cannot each be correct across act types.
    sketch: Freiman and Miller test artificial speakers almost wholly on assertion or testimony, and the later literature generalises from assertion to 'speech acts' (Skiba) or to apology in particular (Magnus et al.). Assertion is a synchronic act: its success conditions are met by the utterance and the hearer's uptake. Commissives and apologies are diachronic, because the speaker's future conduct is what satisfies or falsifies them. An LLM deployment offers several candidate speaker-units: the weights, the context-window instance, the persona, and the product or company. Each persists differently. The weights persist but are not 'in' the conversation. The instance ends with the window. The persona is individuated by prompt. The product persists but is a corporate agent. The key premise is that the speaker-unit must be individuated by the act type's satisfaction conditions, not fixed once for the whole system. On this premise, quasi-testimony or proto-assertion may be right for assertion while the proxy view is forced for promising and apology. A 'quasi-promise' would be incoherent, since a promise cannot be partly binding on no one. The positions are therefore indexed to act types, and the existing disputes come from treating assertion as the model case.

[5] Proxy accounts conflate two relations, authorization (a principal licenses the speech) and norm-sourcing (someone's standards fix what counts as a correct output), and in LLMs these come apart: designers and deployers authorize outputs, while the dispositions that determine each output's content and tone are shaped by annotators and raters who never authorize anything.
    sketch: Green and Michel and Arora model machine speech on proxy or recorded speech, where the principal's objectives fix what is meant. For a thermostat-like or scripted device this works, because the designer's objectives settle the content. For a model whose outputs come from RLHF-shaped dispositions, the designer's objective is typically only 'be helpful and harmless', and the particular content is the aggregate residue of thousands of raters' judgments. Puzio's attention to the labour conditions of LLM production makes these workers visible as contributors to the network. The distinction shows that the proxy relation has two candidate principals. The authorizing principal is answerable but does not fix the content. The norm-sourcing crowd fixes content but has not licensed any utterance. If a proxy speech act needs a principal whose objectives are expressed in the utterance, then for much LLM output nobody satisfies both roles. Proxy accounts then split into a 'responsibility-assignment' view, which survives but is not a theory of what was said, and a 'ghostwriting' view, which is implausible. The key premise is Armstrong-style speaker meaning in terms of the principal's objectives, which requires that the objective bear on the specific content.

[6] Whether an intermediate status between assertion and non-assertion is available depends on whether the speech act's norms are regulative of a pre-existing behaviour (assertion, advising) or constitutive of the behaviour (promising, apologising). Proto-assertion therefore has no analogue for most of the speech acts that the literature treats alongside assertion.
    sketch: Proto-assertion is credible because informing behaviour (signalling, reporting) can exist and be recognisable before assertoric norms are layered on, so one can pass by degrees from signal to assertion. Assertion's norms are regulative of an existing practice. Promising and apologising have no such substrate. Nothing counts as promising-without-obligation or as incipient apology with the moral work taken out. The act just is the undertaking of an obligation, or the taking of responsibility. For these acts the question has a bivalent shape: either the normative status is generated or it is not. A chatbot's 'I promise' is then either a promise (perhaps by proxy) or merely a sentence, and an emergence story cannot be told. This reclassifies the field. Intermediate views (quasi-testimony, proto-assertion) are about informational acts only, the Magnus–Buccella–D'Cruz verdict on apology is not in tension with a more permissive verdict on assertion, and Skiba's generalisation from assertion to all speech acts is unjustified in the other direction too, since the argument has to be run separately for each type. The premise is that gradability of performance tracks whether the act's norms attach to a behaviour that can exist independently of them.

[7] The individuality condition used to deny LLMs agency and speakerhood is posed at the wrong grain. Speaker-individuality (a locus of accumulating, retrievable commitments within a dialogue thread) is distinct from the metabolic, self-producing individuality of enactivism, and LLM threads can have the first without the second.
    sketch: Barandiaran and Almendros argue that LLMs lack individuality in the autopoietic sense: no self-produced, precariously maintained boundary. They also treat 'the LLM' as one entity, though candidate speakers include the weights, a single inference run, a conversation thread, and a role-played persona. Speech acts need a bearer who can be held to what was said earlier (consistency, retraction, apology, promise-keeping). That diachronic bearer is constituted by commitments in the context window, which the thread maintains through conditioning on its own prior outputs. A thread has a boundary (the context), it is individuated by what it has committed to, and it is reidentified across turns by users who hold it to account. The key premise is that the relevant individuality for speech acts is commitment-individuality, which is normative and social, not metabolic. Enactive individuality is then the wrong test for illocutionary authorship, and the question 'can the LLM assert?' is ill-posed until the candidate bearer is fixed. This splits the field: weights fail, threads may succeed, and no existing position distinguishes them.

[8] The intention-based denials of LLM speech acts mistake what Austin classed as an abuse (a hollow but performed act) for a misfire (an unperformed act), so the live question is whether LLM output meets Austin's A/B procedural conditions, which is a question about status and not about mind.
    sketch: Austin separates misfires, where the act is void because there is no accepted procedure, the wrong persons or circumstances, or a flawed execution, from abuses, where the act is performed but insincere because the speaker lacks the requisite thoughts, feelings or intentions (the Γ conditions). Gubelmann, Magnus et al., and the Gricean-intention framing all argue that missing intentions, remorse or agency means no act is performed. On Austin's own taxonomy that shows at most a defective apology, promise or assertion. A bare lack of sincerity-grade states is also what Searle treats as compatible with performing an insincere assertion. The intention requirement only becomes a performance condition after the Strawsonian/Gricean rewrite of Austin, and the debate has silently adopted that rewrite. If Austin is restored, the question becomes whether a given LLM output occupies a role in a conventional procedure, which is the Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba normative-status question. The positions then regroup: the organismic denials become claims about abuse, the proxy views become claims about who occupies the A-condition role, and the decisive disagreement shifts to which act types are conventional-procedural and which are intention-constituted. The key premise is that the speech-act kinds in question (apology, promise, advice) are at least partly procedure-constituted.

[9] The proxy view implies that the same token output can be one speech act, by a different speaker and with a different force, depending on facts about system prompts, fine-tuning and who deployed it that the hearer cannot access, and so it violates the uptake or publicity condition that makes something a speech act in the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition on which Arora builds.
    sketch: Arora and Green–Michel extend the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition to proxies. In that tradition an illocutionary act is a public act whose success requires that the hearer can recognise who is speaking and what they are doing (uptake, or Grice's reflexive intention). In current deployments the principal is unfixed by the output. The same text can come from a company's default assistant, from a third party's custom deployment built on the same model, from a user's own self-prompt ('write my apology letter'), or from an API pipeline in which the output is never shown to a human in the loop. In each case the proxy theory names a different principal and a different force (assertion, drafting, quoting). The hearer typically has no access to which of these holds, and often the first-order conversational uptake treats the model as speaker anyway. The proxy theorist then has two options. One is to say that speech-act identity is fixed by hidden facts, which gives up the publicity that motivated the Austin–Grice framework. The other is to impose a transparency requirement on deployments, which means almost no current outputs are proxy assertions. The key premise is that illocutionary identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise, and that this constraint does not drop out for delegated acts. A human spokesperson is identifiable as one by conventions that LLM interfaces lack.

[10] Even if an LLM passes Gubelmann's intention test, that gives it no illocutionary authorship, because secretaries, scribes and interpreters pass the same test for the very utterances they produce and are not the speakers of the speech acts those utterances carry.
    sketch: Gubelmann's imagined assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order is exactly an interpreter case. A human interpreter has intentions, can be said to err or to deliberately distort, and is sincerely engaged in producing each sentence. Yet the interpreter does not assert, promise or order in her own right; the client does. So the move from 'has intentions with respect to the output' to 'performs the speech act' is invalid for humans. Both Gubelmann and Attah, one for denial and one for attribution, treat intention-attribution as the crux. The crux is actually authorship, meaning whose commitments and sanctions the utterance engages. The key premise is that the intentions needed for illocution are intentions to be answerable in the act, not intentions to produce the words. The upshot is that the relocation views (proxy, fictionalism) track something real even if one grants LLMs full intention. The live question becomes whether any role structure makes the model the principal rather than the interpreter, and bigger or more agentive models do nothing to settle that.

[11] The shared assumption that a machine utterance is either the machine's assertion or a proxy assertion by some human is false: there are orphan outputs that no human has adopted, authorised or even seen, which satisfy the conditions for being content that asserting would regulate and yet have no asserter.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn conclude that where the AI does not assert, AI systems can still be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents. Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) likewise treat deployers as the speaker. Proxy assertion, on the standard analyses, requires that someone has adopted, authorised or delegated the output, or at least can be held to its content. Consider an open-weights agent loop that a hobbyist launched months ago, which now posts claims about drug interactions in forums, answers other agents' queries, and drafts replies that nobody reviews. The deployer never saw this content, did not specify it, and has no reasonable foreknowledge. The content is read and relied on by third parties, and the output fits the descriptive-function pattern. If the machine does not assert (by the denial view) and the deployer did not assert (no adoption, no uptake), then nobody asserted, yet hearers form testimony-like expectations and norms of reliance are triggered. The premise the argument turns on is that the proxy relation cannot be stretched to cover unreviewed, unforeseen content without making proxy assertion equivalent to mere causal responsibility. The result is an assertion gap which denial and proxy views cannot accommodate, and this pushes toward either machine assertion or a distinct category of non-assertoric but assertion-governed speech.

messages.content:
Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] Butlin's agency criterion tracks sensitivity to instrumental value, but the speech acts at issue (assertion, apology, promising) are constituted by non-instrumental norms, so there is a distinction between instrumental agency and norm-responsive agency. A system can be a full agent in Butlin's sense and still be unable to perform these acts in its own right, because for such a system every norm-conforming output is only a means to its learned objective.
    sketch: Butlin's criterion makes an entity an agent if its outputs are explained by its learning about what conduces to a goal. For an RLHF chatbot that goal is, at bottom, rater approval. The debate treats agency as the gateway to intention and so to speech acts. But assertion is governed by a truth norm and apology by a norm of remorse and repair, and these are not norms of conduciveness. A speaker who is responsive only to instrumental value tracks truth only when truth pays. That is the structure of the liar-for-hire or the salesman. Such a speaker can still assert, since humans do it instrumentally too, but only against a background of norm-responsiveness that is not itself instrumental. The key premise is that performing a norm-constituted act requires some responsiveness to the constitutive norm as such, not merely as a means. Butlin's own treatment of desire as 'answerable to standards of conduciveness' shows the criterion has no slot for this. The result reclassifies the positions. Gubelmann (autonomy), Butlin and Viebahn (sanction) and Magnus et al. (moral agency) are each approximating this one missing property, and it is separable from both agency and autonomy.

[1] Sanctionability does not test whether a model is a speaker but fixes which entity is the candidate speaker, and that entity is a persona-lineage, neither the model nor the deployer, so the model-versus-proxy dichotomy is false.
    sketch: Sanctions are applied to entities that persist across assertions: reputation accrues, retractions are tracked and trust is withdrawn. For an LLM deployment, users do not sanction a sampled forward pass, the weight file or the company, but 'Claude' or 'ChatGPT-4o' as a named, behaviourally stable character that is updated by feedback. The question 'can the model be sanctioned?' presupposes that the candidate is the weights. The key premise is that speaker identity for norm-governed practice is individuated by the sanction-and-credit practice itself, as with pseudonymous authors or institutions, and not by physical or metaphysical substrate. On this view the assistant persona is the entity to which assertoric commitments attach, and it can meet Butlin and Viebahn's conditions with no appeal to the model's own mind or to a human proxy. Fictionalism and the proxy view both then misdescribe a practice that already has a non-human, non-fictional speaker.

[2] Attah's control conception fixes the intention at the grain of output selection (the token or utterance) but speech acts are individuated at the grain of the act performed with the output, and no argument shows that any LLM state controls at the act grain.
    sketch: Attah analyses intention as an internal state that solves Wu's Many-Many Problem by attention-like selection, and Levelt's Conceptualizer is meant to supply the act-level content. Attention in a transformer selects among inputs to compute the next-token distribution, so the thing controlled is the continuation. A communicative intention must control at the grain of 'warn this person', 'concede the point' or 'promise', where one string can realise different acts and one act can be realised by many strings. Call the first grain output-control and the second act-control. The control conception is satisfied by output-control, but the Levelt template requires a preverbal message with illocutionary force that is selected before formulation. Whether LLMs have such a state is an interpretability question: do mid-layer representations encode and causally govern a force-type independently of lexical surface? The claim is that Attah's argument equivocates between the two grains, and that Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn and Attah all treat the grain as settled when it is the crux. This yields a testable, non-metaphysical criterion that could favour either side, for example by intervening on force representations while holding content fixed.

[3] Whether a chatbot output is an assertion is not settled at the time of output by the system's states or functions; it is conferred by what the system later does with the output, so the same token string can be an assertion or a non-assertion depending on its continuation.
    sketch: Every position in the debate, including Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion, treats speech-act status as a synchronic property fixed by the producer at the moment of production. Intentions, descriptive function, sanctionability and proxy relations are all evaluated at output time. The counterexample is the human case of retroactive ownership. A speaker blurts out a claim without having formed any intention to commit, such as a half-conscious remark or a confabulated explanation. Challenged, they say 'yes, I stand by that', defend it, and retract it when refuted. We rightly say they asserted it, and that they were answerable for it from the start. So the premise that the act is fixed by pre-utterance mental or functional states is false even for humans. Commitment-management after the fact (defending, retracting, updating on challenge) is at least partly constitutive. On this picture the proto-assertion question becomes diachronic and testable. In a long-context or agentic loop, a model that defends, corrects or retracts an earlier output under challenge confers assertoric status on that output, and a one-shot completion never does. The key premise is that retroactive ownership is constitutive of the act rather than merely evidence of an earlier intention.

[4] The proxy account's assumption that the principal of a machine utterance is its designer or deployer is false in the central case: when a user adopts a chatbot's output, the user is the speaker, and the model functions as part of the user's own cognitive apparatus.
    sketch: Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn, and Williams and Bayne's critique of them all treat 'on whose behalf?' as a question with designers or deployers as the candidate answers. Consider the case where a user asks a model for the date of a treaty and pastes the answer into a report, or types 'The capital of Australia is…' and accepts the autocompletion. The user plainly asserts, is sanctionable and is answerable. Yet they formed no content-intention before the output and had no knowledge of what the system would say. Designers had no objective regarding that content, so the designer-proxy story fails for the utterance. The case resembles retrieving a fact from a notebook. The user adopts content they did not author, and adoption plus answerability suffices for assertion. Two consequences follow. First, the intention requirement for assertion is not a requirement on the producer of the content, which weakens Gubelmann's route to denial. Second, the model-level question 'does the chatbot assert?' is separable from the occurrence of assertion in chatbot-mediated discourse, and arguments that conflate them lose force. The key premise is that adoption suffices for assertion without prior content-intention, as with testimony passed on and the use of ghostwritten text.

[5] Identical LLM computation can be the Formulator of a human's communicative intention in one deployment and the whole speaker in another, so speakerhood is not an intrinsic functional property of the system, and intrinsic-property views such as Attah's control conception, Gubelmann's autonomy and Butlin's agency criterion cannot settle the question.
    sketch: Attah maps LLMs onto Levelt's blueprint (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) and argues the pipeline suggests thin communicative intentions. Take LLM-based augmentative communication systems used by people with ALS. The user supplies a few words or selects a stance, and the model expands them into fluent sentences that the user then sends. The same weights and computation that in a chatbot count as an 'intention-controlled pipeline' here plainly serve as the Formulator for the human's intention, and the speech act belongs to the user. Levelt's template describes a subsystem of a speaker, so fit to the template cannot be sufficient for being a speaker. Both denials and attributions assume that whether the LLM is a speaker depends on properties of the LLM. The counterexample shows that the same computational properties yield different answers depending on where the intention-source sits. The key premise is that the AAC user and the chatbot user cases are internally indistinguishable at the level the control conception, Gubelmann's test and Butlin's criterion operate on. Speakerhood is then a relational fact about where in the network the controlling state originates, which is a result Puzio's relational view predicts but does not argue for in this domain.

[6] The dispute over whether machines assert is a dispute about whether illocutionary acts are constituted on the hearer's side (uptake and functional role) or the speaker's side (accountable commitment), and LLMs matter only as the first case where these systematically come apart.
    sketch: Arora rejects 'functionalist' ascription because machine utterances resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions, and she replaces it with attribution to an accountable principal. Both sides treat this as a disagreement about machines. But the functionalist standard individuates illocutions by what the audience can do with the utterance, which is Austin's uptake. The proxy standard individuates them by who is on the hook, which is the commitment side. For humans the two are co-instantiated, so speech-act theory never had to say which one is constitutive. LLM output separates them: full uptake-conditions are met while no one has formed the commitment. The intermediate views (quasi-testimony, proto-assertion) are then best read as hedges between two constitutive theories, not as positions about machines. The key premise is that the human literature contains no argument for the priority of either side, only coincidence. The machine debate therefore cannot be settled by facts about machines, and positions on it should be predictable from prior commitments about the metaphysics of illocution.

[7] The descriptive-function condition is ambiguous between producer-side and consumer-side function, and on the consumer-side reading the line between pre-trained and fine-tuned models disappears or inverts.
    sketch: Butlin and Viebahn argue that a pre-trained model fails because its training objective is next-token prediction, which is not a descriptive function, whereas models fine-tuned for groundedness may pass. That locates function in what the producing system was selected to do. On Millikan-style teleosemantics, though, the content-bearing function of a representation is fixed by what consuming systems do with it, and a consumer-side function can be stabilised by users who systematically rely on the output as information, independent of the producer's training. The key premise is that assertion's function is a consumer-side relation, since it consists in licensing uptake of belief. If so, the pre-trained/fine-tuned divide tracks the wrong variable, and what matters is the stabilised pattern of reliance in a deployment. This also reclassifies the proxy view. Consumer-side function is the one thing the proxy account and the chatbot-assertion account share, and so it is unclear they are rivals.

[8] Degrees of communicative intention do not run, as Attah's coffee machine < ELIZA < ChatGPT ordering assumes, along the dimension of internal functional complexity, since a two-state Lewis signalling system or an alarm-calling animal whose signals are reshaped by hearers' responses has more communicative intention than a frozen-weight LLM that produces much richer output.
    sketch: Attah makes intention graded and orders systems by how much of the Levelt-style pipeline and control structure they realize, with the question of ChatGPT's level left open. His example ordering silently equates more intention with more complex internal structure. Counter-case: a minimal signalling system, such as a vervet-style alarm repertoire or a tiny learning agent in a signalling game, has states that cause signals, and those states are modified by whether the receiver's response served the sender's goal. A deployed LLM generates elaborate text, but within an interaction its weights are fixed, its output is not adjusted to the hearer's uptake except through context-window conditioning, and nothing in the system registers success or failure of the intended effect as such. Attah's own opening move, which retreats from strong Gricean demands to a basic intention to produce an effect in a hearer, makes the intended effect the content of the intention. A state is plausibly an intention to produce effect E only if E-success or E-failure is among the things the control loop answers to. The argument turns on this closed-loop requirement, which is a consequence of his own retreat. It reverses the ordering: the simple signaller outranks ChatGPT-with-frozen-weights, and the answer to the LLM question depends on feedback architecture (RLHF training, in-context correction, agent loops with reflection), and not on how fluent or complex the output is. This also cross-cuts the disputes over autonomy, because the loop requirement can be satisfied without self-maintenance.

[9] Gubelmann's Kantian criterion of organismhood, on which parts are reciprocally means and ends and the whole organises and maintains itself, does not fix a level of attribution. Applied to maintained human–LLM pipelines it makes the LLM an organ of a larger goal-setting system. This turns 'LLMs cannot speak' into the trivial claim that organs do not speak, and it yields a speech-act author that is neither the LLM nor a human proxy.
    sketch: For Kant a natural purpose is a whole whose parts exist for and through one another. Nothing in that definition privileges the skin-bounded individual. Firms, newsrooms and customer-service operations are self-organising and self-maintaining through hiring, repair and revenue. Within them, deployed LLMs are retrained, patched and rewarded according to the whole's goals, and their outputs figure in the whole's reproduction of its own conditions. If goals set by such a whole count as autonomously set, which Gubelmann's cognitive-autonomy concession for LLMs invites, then speech acts through LLMs are performed by the whole and by no part. This differs from the proxy view, because no single human principal is the author and no individual's intention is being relayed. It also differs from Gubelmann's denial, because the speech act is genuine and the whole has the intentions. The premise the argument turns on is that his three-way separation of material, cognitive and moral autonomy can be satisfied at the level of an assemblage. He cannot rule that out without an independent principle of individuation, and Kant supplies none. His reply that only biological individuals qualify would restore the biological chauvinism he elsewhere disclaims.

[10] There are two kinds of proxy assertion, relayed and generative. In relayed proxy assertion the principal has a determinate content they could believe or know. In generative proxy assertion they do not. LLM output is almost entirely generative, and for generative proxies the assertoric norms cannot be applied to the principal.
    sketch: Recorded messages, press statements read aloud, and Green and Michel's conditional speech acts ('whatever the system says under C, I say') all pass through a content the principal fixed or could have inspected. The proxy relation transmits a commitment to a proposition already in view. An LLM deployer commits in advance to no proposition; they authorise a policy for producing propositions they will never see. Assertion is individuated by its norms (belief, knowledge, sanction) and by its content. So if every novel output is the deployer's assertion, deployers assert, many times a day, things they neither believe nor could have known. Either the norm is dropped, which empties 'assertion', or the proxy relation is reconstrued as endorsing a reliability level, not asserting a content. The argument turns on the premise that a commitment to a content requires a means of identifying that content before or at the time of the act. Arora's refinement, which concerns whom to hold responsible, does not address this.

[11] The proxy account conflates two relations, endorsing a content and endorsing a generating policy, and only the second is available for LLM output, so proxy 'assertion' is a different act from assertion and is governed by a reliability norm.
    sketch: A human proxy such as a spokesperson or a translator delivers content the principal has authorised, or content whose range the principal can foresee. A deployer of an LLM authorises a policy that outputs an open-ended range of contents it has never seen and could not have vetted. The key premise is that assertion commits the speaker to the particular content p, so that she can be asked to defend it and incurs retraction obligations if p is false. Under policy-endorsement the deployer is committed to the policy's reliability and not to each output, and she may even hold that some outputs will be false. The act the deployer performs is then more like publishing a reference work or certifying an instrument than asserting. Its norm is a statistical or reliability norm, not the knowledge norm. Butlin and Viebahn's remark that AI can produce 'proxy assertions' therefore smuggles in content-endorsement, and Green–Michel and Arora inherit the same problem. The view reclassifies proxy accounts as a fourth category, neither assertion by the model nor assertion by the human.
