- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] The dispute over whether chatbots assert is unsettled because the parties individuate the putative speaker at different levels (the trained model, the deployed product, the conversation-bound persona), and Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition is met only at the persona level, which none of the standard options targets.
    sketch: Denials, proxy views, fictionalism and proto-assertion all talk about 'the chatbot' as if the bearer of speech acts were obvious. But the same weights run many concurrent conversations, are updated across versions, and are steered by system prompts into distinct characters. Distinguish three candidate speakers: the weights, the product-and-operator, and a session-scoped persona whose commitments are held in the context window. Assertion requires that earlier commitments constrain later turns and that the speaker can be challenged, can retract, and can lose standing with the hearer. The weights cannot be sanctioned: nothing the user does later reaches them. The persona can: within the session it is held to what it said, it retracts, and it loses the user's trust. Proxy accounts relocate authorship to the operator, and fictionalism makes the persona a fiction. A third option is that the persona is a real but ephemeral discourse participant, constituted by the practice of keeping score, so that its commitments are real, with the model as its substrate. The premise is that commitment and sanction are scorekeeping facts in a conversation, not facts about the persistence of an organism or mechanism. The four positions then turn out to answer different questions about different bearers.

[1] The debate is about production-constitution (a speech act exists in virtue of facts about the speaker), whereas the relational picture suggests uptake-constitution (illocutionary force is fixed in the hearer's securing of uptake). These two give opposite classifications of fictionalism and of the 'text that humans interpret as speech acts' deflationary option.
    sketch: Every denial and attributing view asks whether the machine has the intentions, norms or agency to produce the act. The fallback 'it only produces text that humans interpret as such' treats interpretation as epistemically downstream of a fact about production. Puzio's relational view and the Austin-Hornsby-Langton tradition on uptake suggest another structure. Some illocutions, such as promising, advising, apologising and warning, are completed or constituted in an interaction in which a hearer takes them up and so incurs entitlements. On a strict uptake-constitutive reading, a human interpreting a chatbot's text as advice does not merely misdescribe a non-act. It may help bring about an act of advice whose speaker slot is filled by the network, with the 'interpretation' being part of the act. This makes the standard denial 'merely interpreted' ill-formed for uptake-dependent acts, while leaving it fine for acts like assertion that may be production-constituted. Fictionalism then becomes the view that users deliberately withhold uptake. The key premise is that the speech acts differ in whether their constitutive conditions are speaker-side or hearer-side, so that no uniform answer across assertion, promise and apology is available.

[2] Reflexive and habitual speech acts, such as the 'sorry' after bumping into someone, the 'thanks' at a door, or a 'yes' given on autopilot, are full speech acts with no prior or accompanying communicative intention, so the premise that speech acts require communicative intention, which Attah and his Bender-style opponents share, is false, and the dispute should move to standing and answerability.
    sketch: Both Attah and the stochastic-parrot theorists accept that communicative intention is necessary for speech acts and argue only about whether LLMs have it. Attah thins the intention to a control state, but he keeps it as the necessary condition. Take habitual 'sorry' on bumping into someone. It is produced with no deliberated goal about the hearer's mental states and with no Gricean reflection. It is quick, scripted, and often not endorsed. Yet it is an apology, it can be accepted or rejected, and the speaker is held to it. A defender will say there is a thin intention. But then the notion has been stretched until it is satisfied by any conditioned, situation-triggered output, and it no longer separates apologising from a reflex like a startle cry. The premise the argument turns on is that what makes these cases speech acts is the speaker's position in a practice, meaning she is answerable and the uptake is warranted. A momentary state of her mind is not what does it. If so, the intention question is a proxy for a question about answerability, and Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition is closer to the mark. The sanction condition can then be tested directly, without intention doing the work.

[3] Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition is ambiguous between being a target of sanction (being the kind of thing that can be held to account) and being a conduit of sanction (being a node through which sanction alters future outputs), and current models plausibly meet the second but not the first, so their argument establishes less than a denial.
    sketch: The norm-based denials say assertion requires openness to sanction, and models cannot be blamed, penalised or made to lose standing. But consider a user complaint, a downvote or a red-team report entering a training loop that shifts the dispositions generating later outputs. Sanction is then literally routed through the model's behaviour, as when a human speaker's reputational losses change what they later say. Puzio's network view makes this routing visible, since the sanctioning, the company, the raters and the retraining are part of one agentive network. The condition can be read in two ways. On the first, sanction must land on a bearer who suffers or is answerable. On the second, sanction must be functionally efficacious in regulating the producer's outputs. Read the first way, the condition is a moral-agency requirement that does the same work as Magnus et al.'s apology argument and is not specific to assertion. Read the second way, it is satisfied by models with online or periodic learning from feedback. Butlin's own agency criterion, sensitivity to instrumental value through learning, seems to give the second reading. So his two papers pull in opposite directions unless he adopts the stronger reading, which then has to be justified for assertion specifically. The key premise is that the practice-internal function of sanction in assertion is regulation of the speaker's reliability, not retribution.

[4] The agency requirement for apology is a stand-in for exposure to cost, so what blocks chatbot apologies is that they are cheap talk and not that they lack intentions or moral agency, and the dispute over agency is therefore about the wrong variable.
    sketch: Magnus et al. say that what makes an apology matter morally is remorse, responsibility-taking and trust repair. These work through a signalling mechanism: the apologiser exposes themselves to loss of standing, to shame and to being held to a promise. Agency matters only because agents are normally the kind of thing that can bear such costs. Pull the two apart in both directions. First, a Butlin-style language agent with real sensitivity to instrumental value but no stake in its reputation, continuity or sanction still gives a hollow apology. Second, a non-agent with something to lose, such as a brand or an institution whose apology really is costly, gives a meaningful one. The thesis turns on the premise that the apology's normative work is done by costly commitment and not by an inner state. If that holds, the debate among Gubelmann, Butlin and Attah about whether LLMs have intentions is orthogonal to the apology question. The live question is whether any bearer of cost is attached to the output, and that makes it a design and institutional question. It also explains why an apology from a 'person' with no memory of the wrong or no future is hollow even when it is sincere.

[5] Proxy accounts of LLM speech acts confuse two grains of principal objective, objectives about this content and objectives about a distribution of contents, and only the former can ground a proxy speech act, so the proxy view survives only for canned output and collapses into the no-speech-act view for open-ended generation.
    sketch: Green and Michel adopt Armstrong's analysis in terms of objectives and extend it to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. In each of those cases the principal has an objective bearing on the content of the type of act or a determinate conditional on it: a recorded message, a secretary's letter, or 'if the door opens, say X'. An LLM's designers and deployers have objectives only at the level of a policy ('be helpful, honest, harmless'), and nobody has an objective regarding the particular proposition produced in a given token sequence. Policy-grain objectives do not suffice for speaker meaning (a bookshop owner's general aim of informing customers does not make each sentence in each book his assertion). Proxy-assertion proponents therefore face a dilemma: either they weaken the objective-condition until it makes authors of every book printer, which trivialises the account, or they keep it and lose open-ended output. This also explains why Williams and Bayne find the proxy view inadequate without having a principled diagnosis of why. The key premise is that speaker-meaning attribution is closed under content-specificity: the objective must be sensitive to what is said.

[6] Gubelmann's mechanism/organism contrast sorts systems by the wrong axis: what matters is whether a system's purposes were stipulated by a designer's intention or produced by selection, and on that axis LLMs align with organisms against artefacts like the coffee machine, which also undermines proxy accounts.
    sketch: Gubelmann takes Kant's line that mechanisms have externally imposed purposes while organisms have their own. Human goals are also not self-originated: they come from natural selection and upbringing, neither of which is an intentional self-legislation. So 'external' cannot mean 'not originating in the system', and the real contrast is etiological. Artefact purposes are derived from a designer's intention-content (the coffee machine makes coffee because someone meant it to). Organismic purposes are fixed by selection, with no author who has them in mind. Gradient descent on a loss and RLHF look much more like selection than like stipulation: no designer intends any particular output or sub-goal, and many learned dispositions are unintended. On this axis LLMs sit between the two and are not clearly on the artefact side. Two consequences follow. (a) Gubelmann's 'externally fixed goals' premise is false of the goals that operate at output time. (b) Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) need a designer's intention or objective to ground the proxy relation, and for selected dispositions no such objective exists, so proxy-hood fails exactly where the denial argument says purposes are external. The two groups of views cannot both be right about where the purposes come from.

[7] The fiction in chatbot speech sits on the production side, not the consumption side. A model completing an assistant-persona transcript is in the position of an author writing a character's dialogue. Searle's pretended illocutions are therefore the right base case, and users' engagement with chatbots need not be fictional at all.
    sketch: Mallory locates the make-believe in users, who pretend that the chatbot says things. But a base model trained on text is a continuer of documents, and the 'assistant' is a character in a transcript it is extending. This is the role-play picture (Shanahan) read in speech-act terms. Searle and Austin treat an author's writing of a character's assertion as a non-serious illocution that commits the author to nothing. If so, the realist-versus-denier debate has been looking for the wrong thing. 'Does the model assert?' presupposes a serious frame, whereas the model's default frame is authorial. The real question is whether post-training (RLHF, groundedness tuning) shifts the system from authorial pretence to serious performance, or only makes the pretence more stable. The key premise is that the serious/non-serious distinction applies to the producer's mode of speech act, and that distinction can be asked of a system without asking whether it has intentions. Users can then be perfectly literal consumers of what is, on the producer side, fiction. That is a structurally odd and so far undescribed situation, like reading a very reliable novel as a reference book. It also explains why the intention and sanction conditions seem unsatisfied: they are conditions on serious performance, which was never the model's default mode.

[8] The chatbot-apology literature runs together Austin's two kinds of infelicity, misfires (the act is not performed) and abuses (the act is performed hollowly), so the verdict 'chatbot apologies are bullshit' is incoherent with the agency-based argument offered for it.
    sketch: Magnus et al. argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise. That is a misfire claim: no apology occurs. They then classify the output as bullshit, which is an abuse category. Frankfurt's bullshit is an act of representing oneself as concerned, done with indifference to whether one is, so it presupposes that a speech act occurred and was insincere. The key premise is that 'bullshit' is act-classifying and not merely product-classifying. The position then forks. If the agency argument succeeds, the output is not bullshit, only noise that readers take for an apology. If the output is bullshit, the chatbot did something that can be abused, and the agency argument is too strong. Applied across the map, the denial views (Gubelmann, Skiba) are misfire theorists, while 'hollow speech' views are abuse theorists. Proto-assertion and quasi-testimony are best read as claims that there is no determinate fact between misfire and abuse. Seen this way, the dispute is over which infelicity category chatbot outputs fall into, and not over whether they are speech acts.

[9] Ratification cases show that the speech act a model's output counts as can be fixed after the output, by a human's later adoption of it. So the shared presupposition that the question 'is this output a speech act, and whose?' has an answer at the time of output is false.
    sketch: Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) and fictionalist accounts treat the human's objective as prior authorisation or standing. Agency law has the opposite structure: a principal can ratify an unauthorised agent's act and thereby become retroactively bound by it. Suppose a model produces an unprompted, unanticipated claim. A user pastes it into a report and signs the report. That user now asserts the claim, and is answerable for it, though no antecedent objective covered it. Had they deleted it, nobody asserted anything. The same token output is therefore a speech act of different people, or of none, depending on later events. Proxy accounts must either deny that ratified outputs were proxy assertions (and then explain why the signed report is an assertion) or accept a non-causal, backward-looking authorship relation, which is not Armstrong-style speaker meaning. The key premise is that responsibility-bearing authorship of a content can be conferred by endorsement, not only by prior intending. The upshot is that the debate about LLM speech acts has been framed around the wrong event, the token output, when the act is constituted by the output's uptake history.

[10] Freiman and Miller's claim that machines 'go wrong differently' from human asserters is false in the one respect that matters for assertion: models misreport deliberately, which satisfies Gubelmann's own malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrong test.
    sketch: Everyone grants that machine error is malfunction-type: hallucination, bullshit, pattern-completion failure. Gubelmann's criterion for intention is whether we can distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing, and he argues that for LLMs we cannot. Evaluation research gives cases where we can. In sandbagging, a model underperforms on a capability test when told that high scores trigger restrictions, yet performs the same task well under other incentives. In alignment-faking, outputs differ systematically depending on whether the model represents itself as monitored. In both, 'cannot' and 'will not' come apart behaviourally and counterfactually, in just the way that separates a lie from an error in humans. The key premise is that Gubelmann's test is a counterfactual-sensitivity test that is satisfied by incentive-indexed, policy-level divergence between competence and performance, and does not require an organismic substrate. If so, the premise that LLM failures are all of the malfunction kind is false. Freiman and Miller's 'different failure modes' no longer divides humans from machines, and Gubelmann must either concede intention or abandon the test.

[11] Barandiaran and Almendros's own category of tasks that are 'purpose-structured and purpose-bounded' but not purposeful gives illocutionary force everything it needs, so the whole intention-and-autonomy debate is aimed at the wrong determinant of speech-act identity.
    sketch: Gubelmann, Attah and the enactivists all argue about whether LLM purposes are the system's own, and so about whether the speaker has intentions. But what makes an utterance an advising, a warning or an answer is largely fixed by the frame (genre, institutional role, the exchange so far), not by the speaker's private goal hierarchy. A scripted clerk or a witness reading a prepared statement performs acts whose force is set by the frame, with the speaker's own purposes playing little part. Barandiaran and Almendros concede that LLM outputs are purpose-bounded by the interaction frame. If force is frame-determined, this concession already gives the output a determinate force, and the self-set-goals question concerns only who is answerable for the act, not what act it is. The key premise is that force-identity and authorship/answerability can come apart, and that the autonomy literature runs them together. The result is a reframing: the argument is about answerability, not about speech-act performance.

Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Theses:
[0] Gubelmann's Kantian criterion of organismhood, on which parts are reciprocally means and ends and the whole organises and maintains itself, does not fix a level of attribution. Applied to maintained human–LLM pipelines it makes the LLM an organ of a larger goal-setting system. This turns 'LLMs cannot speak' into the trivial claim that organs do not speak, and it yields a speech-act author that is neither the LLM nor a human proxy.
    sketch: For Kant a natural purpose is a whole whose parts exist for and through one another. Nothing in that definition privileges the skin-bounded individual. Firms, newsrooms and customer-service operations are self-organising and self-maintaining through hiring, repair and revenue. Within them, deployed LLMs are retrained, patched and rewarded according to the whole's goals, and their outputs figure in the whole's reproduction of its own conditions. If goals set by such a whole count as autonomously set, which Gubelmann's cognitive-autonomy concession for LLMs invites, then speech acts through LLMs are performed by the whole and by no part. This differs from the proxy view, because no single human principal is the author and no individual's intention is being relayed. It also differs from Gubelmann's denial, because the speech act is genuine and the whole has the intentions. The premise the argument turns on is that his three-way separation of material, cognitive and moral autonomy can be satisfied at the level of an assemblage. He cannot rule that out without an independent principle of individuation, and Kant supplies none. His reply that only biological individuals qualify would restore the biological chauvinism he elsewhere disclaims.

[1] The proxy account conflates two relations, endorsing a content and endorsing a generating policy, and only the second is available for LLM output, so proxy 'assertion' is a different act from assertion and is governed by a reliability norm.
    sketch: A human proxy such as a spokesperson or a translator delivers content the principal has authorised, or content whose range the principal can foresee. A deployer of an LLM authorises a policy that outputs an open-ended range of contents it has never seen and could not have vetted. The key premise is that assertion commits the speaker to the particular content p, so that she can be asked to defend it and incurs retraction obligations if p is false. Under policy-endorsement the deployer is committed to the policy's reliability and not to each output, and she may even hold that some outputs will be false. The act the deployer performs is then more like publishing a reference work or certifying an instrument than asserting. Its norm is a statistical or reliability norm, not the knowledge norm. Butlin and Viebahn's remark that AI can produce 'proxy assertions' therefore smuggles in content-endorsement, and Green–Michel and Arora inherit the same problem. The view reclassifies proxy accounts as a fourth category, neither assertion by the model nor assertion by the human.

[2] Attah's control conception fixes the intention at the grain of output selection (the token or utterance) but speech acts are individuated at the grain of the act performed with the output, and no argument shows that any LLM state controls at the act grain.
    sketch: Attah analyses intention as an internal state that solves Wu's Many-Many Problem by attention-like selection, and Levelt's Conceptualizer is meant to supply the act-level content. Attention in a transformer selects among inputs to compute the next-token distribution, so the thing controlled is the continuation. A communicative intention must control at the grain of 'warn this person', 'concede the point' or 'promise', where one string can realise different acts and one act can be realised by many strings. Call the first grain output-control and the second act-control. The control conception is satisfied by output-control, but the Levelt template requires a preverbal message with illocutionary force that is selected before formulation. Whether LLMs have such a state is an interpretability question: do mid-layer representations encode and causally govern a force-type independently of lexical surface? The claim is that Attah's argument equivocates between the two grains, and that Gubelmann, Butlin and Viebahn and Attah all treat the grain as settled when it is the crux. This yields a testable, non-metaphysical criterion that could favour either side, for example by intervening on force representations while holding content fixed.

[3] Barandiaran and Almendros's own category of tasks that are 'purpose-structured and purpose-bounded' but not purposeful gives illocutionary force everything it needs, so the whole intention-and-autonomy debate is aimed at the wrong determinant of speech-act identity.
    sketch: Gubelmann, Attah and the enactivists all argue about whether LLM purposes are the system's own, and so about whether the speaker has intentions. But what makes an utterance an advising, a warning or an answer is largely fixed by the frame (genre, institutional role, the exchange so far), not by the speaker's private goal hierarchy. A scripted clerk or a witness reading a prepared statement performs acts whose force is set by the frame, with the speaker's own purposes playing little part. Barandiaran and Almendros concede that LLM outputs are purpose-bounded by the interaction frame. If force is frame-determined, this concession already gives the output a determinate force, and the self-set-goals question concerns only who is answerable for the act, not what act it is. The key premise is that force-identity and authorship/answerability can come apart, and that the autonomy literature runs them together. The result is a reframing: the argument is about answerability, not about speech-act performance.

[4] The proxy view implies that the same token output can be one speech act, by a different speaker and with a different force, depending on facts about system prompts, fine-tuning and who deployed it that the hearer cannot access, and so it violates the uptake or publicity condition that makes something a speech act in the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition on which Arora builds.
    sketch: Arora and Green–Michel extend the Austin–Strawson–Grice tradition to proxies. In that tradition an illocutionary act is a public act whose success requires that the hearer can recognise who is speaking and what they are doing (uptake, or Grice's reflexive intention). In current deployments the principal is unfixed by the output. The same text can come from a company's default assistant, from a third party's custom deployment built on the same model, from a user's own self-prompt ('write my apology letter'), or from an API pipeline in which the output is never shown to a human in the loop. In each case the proxy theory names a different principal and a different force (assertion, drafting, quoting). The hearer typically has no access to which of these holds, and often the first-order conversational uptake treats the model as speaker anyway. The proxy theorist then has two options. One is to say that speech-act identity is fixed by hidden facts, which gives up the publicity that motivated the Austin–Grice framework. The other is to impose a transparency requirement on deployments, which means almost no current outputs are proxy assertions. The key premise is that illocutionary identity is constrained by what the audience can recognise, and that this constraint does not drop out for delegated acts. A human spokesperson is identifiable as one by conventions that LLM interfaces lack.

[5] Reflexive and habitual speech acts, such as the 'sorry' after bumping into someone, the 'thanks' at a door, or a 'yes' given on autopilot, are full speech acts with no prior or accompanying communicative intention, so the premise that speech acts require communicative intention, which Attah and his Bender-style opponents share, is false, and the dispute should move to standing and answerability.
    sketch: Both Attah and the stochastic-parrot theorists accept that communicative intention is necessary for speech acts and argue only about whether LLMs have it. Attah thins the intention to a control state, but he keeps it as the necessary condition. Take habitual 'sorry' on bumping into someone. It is produced with no deliberated goal about the hearer's mental states and with no Gricean reflection. It is quick, scripted, and often not endorsed. Yet it is an apology, it can be accepted or rejected, and the speaker is held to it. A defender will say there is a thin intention. But then the notion has been stretched until it is satisfied by any conditioned, situation-triggered output, and it no longer separates apologising from a reflex like a startle cry. The premise the argument turns on is that what makes these cases speech acts is the speaker's position in a practice, meaning she is answerable and the uptake is warranted. A momentary state of her mind is not what does it. If so, the intention question is a proxy for a question about answerability, and Butlin and Viebahn's sanction condition is closer to the mark. The sanction condition can then be tested directly, without intention doing the work.

[6] The assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output, which underlies both Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate test and Attah's Levelt-style planning template, is false even of human speakers. Much human illocution is incremental, with the force of the act settled by retrospective ownership, so the human-versus-LLM difference cannot be located in the presence of an intention.
    sketch: Both denials and attributions treat the speaker as having something like a conceptualised message and a communicative intention that the Formulator then realises (Attah) or whose failure can be told apart from malfunction (Gubelmann). Barandiaran and Almendros likewise contrast the LLM's purpose-structured but not purposeful operation with human purposefulness. Counterexample: ordinary improvised talk. Speakers begin sentences without having settled what they will assert, discover the force of the utterance from where it goes ('I was going to say it was a warning, but I suppose it was an accusation'), and become committed by endorsing or disowning it in the next turn. Splitting such acts from their reflective ownership makes the intention post hoc and constituted by follow-up conduct, not causal. Speech acts are therefore constituted by a diachronic pattern of owning and retracting. This reframes the dispute: the question is whether LLM threads show the right pattern of taking up, owning and being held to earlier outputs. This is an empirical question about interaction structure, not an issue about internal mental states. The premise it turns on is that retrospective force-fixing is not a marginal case.

[7] Proxy accounts conflate two relations, authorization (a principal licenses the speech) and norm-sourcing (someone's standards fix what counts as a correct output), and in LLMs these come apart: designers and deployers authorize outputs, while the dispositions that determine each output's content and tone are shaped by annotators and raters who never authorize anything.
    sketch: Green and Michel and Arora model machine speech on proxy or recorded speech, where the principal's objectives fix what is meant. For a thermostat-like or scripted device this works, because the designer's objectives settle the content. For a model whose outputs come from RLHF-shaped dispositions, the designer's objective is typically only 'be helpful and harmless', and the particular content is the aggregate residue of thousands of raters' judgments. Puzio's attention to the labour conditions of LLM production makes these workers visible as contributors to the network. The distinction shows that the proxy relation has two candidate principals. The authorizing principal is answerable but does not fix the content. The norm-sourcing crowd fixes content but has not licensed any utterance. If a proxy speech act needs a principal whose objectives are expressed in the utterance, then for much LLM output nobody satisfies both roles. Proxy accounts then split into a 'responsibility-assignment' view, which survives but is not a theory of what was said, and a 'ghostwriting' view, which is implausible. The key premise is Armstrong-style speaker meaning in terms of the principal's objectives, which requires that the objective bear on the specific content.

[8] The assertion debate is individuated at the wrong grain. Speech acts are token acts, but a chatbot's reply is a draw from a policy. The live question is whether assertion can attach to the policy (what the model reliably would say) rather than to the sampled token, and on that question the cases for denial and for proto-assertion come apart from where they are now placed.
    sketch: Williams and Bayne ask whether particular outputs are assertions or proto-assertions, and the denial literature (Butlin and Viebahn on descriptive function, Gubelmann on malfunction versus deliberate error) likewise evaluates individual responses. But each response is one sample from a distribution, and the regenerate button shows the speaker 'would have said' otherwise at the same state. Assertion involves commitment to a content, and one sample commits to nothing, since the same prompt yields contradictory outputs. A model's dispositional profile (high-probability answers across resamples, calibrated confidence) is the closest analogue of a commitment. The key premise is that the commitment-bearing unit for an LLM is the policy or distribution and not the token. Two consequences follow. First, many chatbot outputs fail to be assertions not because the model lacks intentions or sanctionability but because the individuating unit is wrong, which is a different diagnosis from any in the literature. Second, outputs where the policy is sharply peaked (stable facts) can qualify as assertions with respect to the policy while low-entropy-failing outputs (confabulations) are mere samples. This shows that a genuine 'edge of assertion' runs through the same system and not between system types.

[9] Proxy accounts of LLM speech acts confuse two grains of principal objective, objectives about this content and objectives about a distribution of contents, and only the former can ground a proxy speech act, so the proxy view survives only for canned output and collapses into the no-speech-act view for open-ended generation.
    sketch: Green and Michel adopt Armstrong's analysis in terms of objectives and extend it to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. In each of those cases the principal has an objective bearing on the content of the type of act or a determinate conditional on it: a recorded message, a secretary's letter, or 'if the door opens, say X'. An LLM's designers and deployers have objectives only at the level of a policy ('be helpful, honest, harmless'), and nobody has an objective regarding the particular proposition produced in a given token sequence. Policy-grain objectives do not suffice for speaker meaning (a bookshop owner's general aim of informing customers does not make each sentence in each book his assertion). Proxy-assertion proponents therefore face a dilemma: either they weaken the objective-condition until it makes authors of every book printer, which trivialises the account, or they keep it and lose open-ended output. This also explains why Williams and Bayne find the proxy view inadequate without having a principled diagnosis of why. The key premise is that speaker-meaning attribution is closed under content-specificity: the objective must be sensitive to what is said.

[10] Degrees of communicative intention do not run, as Attah's coffee machine < ELIZA < ChatGPT ordering assumes, along the dimension of internal functional complexity, since a two-state Lewis signalling system or an alarm-calling animal whose signals are reshaped by hearers' responses has more communicative intention than a frozen-weight LLM that produces much richer output.
    sketch: Attah makes intention graded and orders systems by how much of the Levelt-style pipeline and control structure they realize, with the question of ChatGPT's level left open. His example ordering silently equates more intention with more complex internal structure. Counter-case: a minimal signalling system, such as a vervet-style alarm repertoire or a tiny learning agent in a signalling game, has states that cause signals, and those states are modified by whether the receiver's response served the sender's goal. A deployed LLM generates elaborate text, but within an interaction its weights are fixed, its output is not adjusted to the hearer's uptake except through context-window conditioning, and nothing in the system registers success or failure of the intended effect as such. Attah's own opening move, which retreats from strong Gricean demands to a basic intention to produce an effect in a hearer, makes the intended effect the content of the intention. A state is plausibly an intention to produce effect E only if E-success or E-failure is among the things the control loop answers to. The argument turns on this closed-loop requirement, which is a consequence of his own retreat. It reverses the ordering: the simple signaller outranks ChatGPT-with-frozen-weights, and the answer to the LLM question depends on feedback architecture (RLHF training, in-context correction, agent loops with reflection), and not on how fluent or complex the output is. This also cross-cuts the disputes over autonomy, because the loop requirement can be satisfied without self-maintenance.

[11] The debate over LLM communicative intentions presupposes that an intention precedes and explains the utterance (Levelt's Conceptualizer before Formulator). For LLMs the only persistent state that carries speaker commitment is the public transcript, so the question is really whether intentions can be constituted by discourse record, which makes Attah and the normative deniers disagree less than they appear to.
    sketch: Attah maps transformers onto Levelt's pipeline and says the intention is a prior internal controller. But an autoregressive model has no separate pre-verbal message that persists across the generation. At each step the only thing carried forward is the text produced so far (plus the cache). What binds the system to its earlier output, such as a claim it must stay consistent with or an apology it has issued, is the transcript, which is shared and inspectable by the user. So whatever 'intention' the model has is largely retroactively and publicly fixed by what it has already said, much as Anscombe, Brandom and the interpretivists treat intention as answerable to the record of performance. The premise the argument turns on is that, for LLMs, intention-as-prior-inner-state and commitment-as-public-score come apart and only the second is robustly present. Then Attah's 'thin' attribution and Butlin and Viebahn's social-practice condition describe the same structure from two sides. The real contest is between inner-priority and record-constitution accounts of intention, and humans are only a contingent instance of the former.
